mutants.title: Outsourced Large-Load Intake Desk for Co-op Pools
mutants.one_liner: A stage-gated, applicant-paid intake administrator and cross-utility duplicate registry for G&T co-op pools outside ERCOT, so 5-person planning staffs only ever see evidence-backed projects.
mutants.customer: Wedge: one mid-size G&T (or state co-op association planning group) outside ERCOT, in SPP, MISO or the Mountain West, that fields 8+ large-load inquiries a year and has 1-2 planners eating the load (Central Electric Power Cooperative's lead spends about 40% of his time on data centers). The G&T adopts the desk by board resolution, and the applicant pays through a filed fee schedule, following Great River Energy's bill-the-petitioner model. Second ring: the G&T's 20-40 distribution co-ops, then neighboring G&Ts.
mutants.problem: The judges' central worry was right. Collateral, study fees and site-control rules are making applicants self-prove, so a 12-point memo shop sells checks the applicant will soon hand over anyway. Equipment slots and financing letters are also confidential, and real developers often call the utility before they order equipment. Meanwhile the co-op still has no staff to run intake and no way to see that the same 300 MW is being shopped to five utilities. Regulators are absorbing LLC transparency at the state level (Texas audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 order for projects over 25 MW), which weakens any pure-LLC-lookup product.
mutants.solution: Run intake as an operated service, not a memo. (1) Evidence ladder tied to money release. Gate 0 (intake fee paid): public-record checks only, which is what any real developer already has: LLC principals across states, recorded deed or option, air-permit pre-application and generator count vs. claimed MW, water and stormwater filings, and claimed energization date vs. published transformer and switchgear lead times. Gate 1 (study deposit released): named references (OEM, EPC, tenant, lender officer) verified by phone, with a signed attestation and a misrepresentation clause that forfeits the deposit. Gate 2 (ESA signature): redacted OEM order acknowledgment and financing confirmation. Early gates test only what an early-stage real project has; unobservable items are pushed to the gate where money is at risk. (2) Consent clause: the application form has the applicant consent to share LLC, principals, parcel APN, POI substation, MW ask and status with a pooled registry, which solves the confidentiality problem. The registry matches on parcel, substation POI and principal, not company name, because shells rename themselves but land parcels and substations do not. It returns hits like 'this parcel and principal appear in 3 other territories.' (3) Outputs are structured records that drop into GridUnity or PowerClerk as the pre-queue front door.
mutants.why_now: Tariffs and collateral rules are landing (Texas SB 6 final rule due by 12/31/2026, AEP Ohio-style deposits), and Exelon's pipeline fell about 40% and AEP Ohio's more than half once fees and collateral arrived. Every co-op now has to decide what its intake rules are, and most have no staff to run them. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so boards are burned. Cleanview-class permit data has made the public-record layer cheap to assemble and license. Nobody yet runs a duplicate registry outside ERCOT, where SB 6 mandates duplicate disclosure only inside the state.
mutants.revenue_model: $20-30K one-time G&T setup (intake policy, fee schedule, ESA rider, board presentation). Applicant-paid intake fees scaled by MW, $10K under 100 MW up to $40K over 500 MW, plus a $15-30K Gate 1 verification fee. The utility keeps a 15% admin share and the desk keeps 85%. A $36K/yr G&T floor retainer covers slow quarters. Registry seats at $12K/yr for utilities outside the pool later. Bottom-up: 3 G&Ts x about 25 paid intakes x about $20K is $1.5M in year 1 at about 80% gross margin, with the registry as the compounding asset.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The fee and the gates are themselves the phantom filter. Shell LLCs will not pay $15K to be verified, and real developers spending $2B+ will not blink. So the desk's real product is converting scarce planner hours into a queue that carries only evidence-backed projects, and detection is a side effect. The staged ladder fixes the 'real developers come before they order equipment' flaw by demanding equipment proof only at the gate where the utility's money is at risk. And the registry keys on parcels and POI substations, physical objects a phantom cannot rename, which is why it holds up even as LLC-disclosure rules improve.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: get the last 10-15 inquiries from two co-op contacts via a state association or G&T planning group. Back-test them to show how the ones that died would have scored at Gate 0 and Gate 1. Stand up scrapers for air-permit databases in 4-6 states and deed and Secretary of State records in 2-3 territories, and license Cleanview-style permit data instead of rebuilding it. Days 10-20: write the 2-page intake policy, fee schedule and misrepresentation-clause template. Present the back-test and template to the G&T planning head and ask for a 90-day pilot that starts fees on the next new inquiry, free for existing ones. Days 20-30: interview 5 developers with real projects to test that they would pay $10-15K at intake. Close 1 G&T pilot and process the first paid intake. Kill test: if no G&T will let applicants be billed, or 0 of 5 real developers accept the fee, the applicant-pays thesis is dead.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GridUnity and PowerClerk are workflow tools built on applicant-supplied data. The desk verifies and feeds them as a front door, so it is a complement to sell alongside, not a rival. Enverus, LandGate, GridCARE and ZEG sit on the developer side or in forecasting, and this desk works for the utility and is adverse to the applicant. Cleanview is a public tracker and cannot hold confidential cross-utility inquiry data, so it becomes a licensed input rather than a competitor. NRECA offers free checklists but cannot run a fee-collecting, data-holding, liability-bearing intake operation, so its state associations are the resale channel. Hourly consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) could copy the checks but not the pooled registry economics. Memos were the entry product; the pooled registry across co-ops is the business, and it gets better with every co-op added.

mutants.title: Phantom Pipeline Audits for Utility Rate-Case Intervenors
mutants.one_liner: Sell to the ratepayers who pay for phantom load, meaning industrial customer groups and state consumer advocates in IRP, CPCN and large-load-tariff dockets, a testimony-ready audit of how much of a utility's confidential data-center pipeline is physically real.
mutants.customer: Buyer: counsel and expert budgets of (a) industrial customer intervenor groups (steel, paper, chemicals) that fear being left with stranded data-center infrastructure costs, and (b) state consumer advocate offices, in dockets where the utility's generation or transmission request rests on a data-center pipeline. Later: county and city governments facing abatement votes ($15-30K packs), and utility credit and equity analysts who subscribe to a Phantom Ratio Index. The sales path is through the law firms and staff attorneys who run these dockets.
mutants.problem: Utilities are asking commissions to approve gigawatts of gas plants and transmission justified by 'signed' large-load pipelines. The pipeline exhibits are confidential or anonymized ('Customer A, 400 MW'). Intervenor experts can only critique them top-down with econometrics, because nobody checks entries one by one against the physical trail. The evidence that pipelines are inflated is broad: an EPRI survey found none of 10 utilities with requests of 50%+ of peak expected actual 5-year load above 35% of peak, and Exelon's estimates fell about 40% after stricter collateral. But the intervenor cannot show which megawatts are fake, and a project shopped to two utilities is counted twice.
mutants.solution: A 'realization audit' delivered through counsel. Under the docket's protective order, the desk takes the utility's pipeline exhibit (MW, county or substation, in-service date, status). It scores each entry against the public trail: air permits and generator counts, deed or option and rezoning agenda items, water and stormwater filings, principal and LLC cross-matching across states, and whether the claimed in-service date is feasible given published equipment lead times. The output is a probability-weighted realized MW by year with confidence bands, a list of duplicate-counted megawatts across utilities, and a testimony-ready exhibit sponsored by a credentialed expert witness (a retired utility planner or former commission staffer on retainer). Where entries are fully anonymized, the audit triangulates from county-level permit and land-use activity and asks the commission to compel the identities under protective order. The same work product seeds a quarterly Phantom Ratio Index by utility and state.
mutants.why_now: Electricity affordability is a live political issue in the November 2026 midterms, and data-center load forecasts are the key contested input in a wave of 2026 large-load tariff, IRP and generation-certificate dockets. Regulators are already moving on transparency (Texas ownership audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW), so intervenors now have standing to ask for pipeline detail. Cleanview-style permit trackers plus OCR'd county records have made the public-trail checks cheap enough to run per docket at a fixed fee.
mutants.revenue_model: $40-120K fixed fee per docket engagement, covering the audit, exhibit and expert sponsorship, paid from intervenor budgets and industrial group dues. $15-30K county and municipal packs. A $25-60K/yr Phantom Ratio Index seat for credit analysts, muni and equity desks and hedge funds. Year-1 target: 6-10 dockets ($600K-$900K) plus early index subscribers, with about 60% gross margin because the expert and analyst time is billable.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The parties who lose most from phantom load are not the utility's five planners but the other ratepayers, and they already have lawyers, a procedural calendar and an expert budget. The docket schedule sets the deadline, so no procurement cycle is needed. The natural competitors, utility-aligned engineering consultancies, are conflicted when the audit target is their client's pipeline, which makes an adversarial audit counter-positioned rather than just different. And duplicate-counting is only visible from outside: each utility sees only its own queue, but an auditor working in four states sees the same project in three pipelines. The adversarial work therefore seeds the national duplicate registry from a side no utility-aligned vendor can reach.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every live docket in 6-8 states where a large-load pipeline is in dispute, using public commission dockets, and note testimony deadlines in the next 60-120 days plus who the intervenors and their counsel are. Days 10-20: build a free 2-page 'public trail check' of one utility's publicly disclosed data-center announcements, using licensed permit data plus deeds and permits, and send it to 15 intervenor counsel and consumer advocate staff. Recruit a credentialed expert witness (retired planner or ex-commission staff). Days 20-30: close 1-2 paid engagements at about $40K, one with an industrial group and one with a consumer advocate. Kill test: if counsel will not pay $40K for a per-entry audit because their econometric expert already covers it, the intervenor thesis is dead and the index is the fallback.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GridUnity, PowerClerk, Camus and Ascend sell software to utilities as vendors, run on applicant-supplied data and cannot be adversarial. Enverus (load forecasting for utilities), LandGate and GridCARE serve utilities or developers. Cleanview is a free tracker with no per-entry audit, expert witness or confidential pipeline access, so it is a data input, not a rival. ZEG advises developers and utilities. NRECA serves co-ops and has nothing for IOU dockets. Utility-aligned consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) are conflicted by their clients, and existing intervenor-side experts do top-down forecast critique, not entry-level physical-trail verification. The buyer, the payer and the deliverable are all different from the parent's co-op memo, so nobody in the parent's research is selling to the same person.

mutants.title: Megawatt Credit Bureau with Bonded Collateral
mutants.one_liner: Invert the vetting desk: real developers pay to be rated, utilities accept the rating for lower deposits, and the company eventually underwrites large-load security bonds off the physical-readiness data, so regulators' collateral rules become the market instead of the threat.
mutants.customer: First payer: mid-size and regional developers with real sites and real equipment slots (powered-land developers, ex-bitcoin-miner sites converting to AI, regional colo builders) that are in 10-30 utility queues and being asked for $50K/MW collateral or up to $100K per study in each. Accepting side: co-op and municipal pools that agree to recognize the rating. Capital side: a specialty surety or insurance carrier and reinsurer that provide bond capacity through an MGA structure.
mutants.problem: Collateral regimes (Texas proposes $50K/MW, AEP Ohio-style deposits) treat every applicant as a phantom. A real 300 MW project must lock up $15M in cash or letters of credit per utility, and re-submit the same package to each co-op. Hyperscaler-backed developers have the balance sheet and shells do not, so thinly capitalized developers with real projects get squeezed or forced to sell to bigger players. Surety and LC markets price the principal's balance sheet, not the project's physical readiness, so there is no credit signal between a hyperscaler guarantee and a shell LLC. Utilities cannot tell the difference either.
mutants.solution: Phase 1 (months 0-6): the 'Verified Ready' dossier for $15-25K. The developer hands over what real projects have (air permit, deed or option, OEM slot confirmation, EPC contract, tenant LOI, financing letter), and the desk verifies it through public records and direct confirmation calls. It issues a dated, registry-anchored readiness rating (R1-R5) that pilot co-op pools accept as satisfying Gates 0-1 and as grounds for a 30-50% deposit reduction or study priority. Utilities pay nothing. Phase 2 (months 6-18): a bonded-collateral program, meaning surety-style 'large-load security bonds' written by a specialty carrier through an MGA, priced off the rating and posted to the utility as obligee in place of part of the cash or LC collateral. Phase 3: publish the methodology as an open standard and lobby tariffs and regulators to reference it, e.g. 'rated applicants may post bonds or reduced collateral.' The registry accumulates milestone-hit data on who actually energizes, which becomes proprietary loss data no one else has.
mutants.why_now: Texas SB 6 (final rule due by 12/31/2026), AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs and study fees of up to $100K created a huge new collateral requirement that did not exist 18 months ago, and each dollar of required cash collateral creates demand for a cheaper substitute. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 make equipment evidence a cheap, hard-to-fake readiness signal that a rating can be built on. Roughly half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities and lenders are hunting for a credible signal.
mutants.revenue_model: Rating fee $15-25K (up to $75K per GW) per developer per accepting utility set, plus $5K/yr renewals. Bond premium of 2-3% a year on the security amount, with the MGA taking about 20-25% commission plus profit share and the carrier taking the risk. Later, registry data licences to lenders and utilities. Illustrative: 40 rated projects in year 1 is about $800K. At 100 bonded projects a year with $15M average security, that is $1.5B of security, about $37M of premium and about $9M of MGA revenue. It rises further if regulators adopt the rating in tariffs.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Regulators' collateral rules look like the death of a vetting business, but they are the birth of a substitute market, and a substitute needs an underwriter that can price physical readiness. The paying base self-selects to real projects because phantoms will not pay to be scrutinized. The classic conflict of interest of issuer-paid ratings is solved by having the MGA and carrier carry loss exposure, so the rater has skin in the game, unlike a ratings shop. Finally, the segment nobody serves is the thin-balance-sheet developer with real equipment slots, whose risk is legible only in the logistics trail. The rating therefore turns a compliance cost into a moat: loss data on who energizes.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 15 mid-size developers, sourced from the 384 developers on Cleanview's tracker, powered-land brokers and LinkedIn, asking how many co-op queues they are in, how much collateral is posted and how many times they have re-submitted. Days 10-20: pre-sell 3 dossiers at a $10K founding price, refundable if no co-op accepts. Use the free co-op back-test as the lead magnet to sign an MOU with one G&T pool to accept the dossier for deposit relief. Draft methodology v0.1 and publish it openly. Days 20-30: talk to 2 commercial surety brokers or MGAs that already place utility deposit bonds and get term-sheet-level interest, not a binder. Deliver the first dossier. Kill test: if no G&T will trade a rating for lower deposits, the utility-acceptance leg fails and the bond phase never starts.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GridUnity and PowerClerk are utility workflow tools, and the rating is a credential they can ingest. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE help developers pick sites or find capacity but do not verify readiness or produce a rating a utility will accept for lower deposits. Cleanview is a public tracker with no verification or credential. ZEG is advisory consulting. NRECA is a distribution channel that can endorse the standard but cannot underwrite. A two-sided credential (developers pay, utilities accept) that later carries insurance-backed loss data has network and data economics none of them touch, and the parent's own problem, that collateral rules substitute for vetting, is turned into the demand driver.

mutants.title: Independent Auditor for AI-Paid Pet Claims
mutants.one_liner: A read-only shadow adjudicator plus a cross-carrier duplicate registry that independently re-checks every auto-paid pet claim against the policy's own clauses and produces the validation records state examiners now ask for.
mutants.customer: Head of claims and the compliance officer at US pet-insurance MGAs and small carriers paying roughly 100k-400k claims a year that already auto-adjudicate through a vendor platform or in-house LLM triage. The channel is the fronting carriers whose binders give them claims-audit rights over those MGAs. Narrowest wedge: MGAs that announced automation in the last 18 months and write in the 25+ states that have adopted the NAIC AI bulletin.
mutants.problem: Once claims are auto-paid, the insurer is accountable for the model's output but cannot see inside it, and the vendor selling the automation is marking its own homework. Two failures are invisible. One is silent overpayment: excluded lines paid (exam fees, cremation, prescription diets, supplements), wrong deductible, co-insurance, annual-limit or waiting-period math. The other is wrongful denial, which means complaints and market-conduct exposure. No single carrier can see the same PDF invoice filed with two insurers, or an altered invoice that looks fine in isolation. The parent's price-based edits add a third problem: reductions land on owners as balance bills, with no vet contract behind them, so mid-size insurers will not fund them.
mutants.solution: Read-only nightly export of invoice, policy form and adjudication decision, with no workflow replacement. (1) Normalize every invoice line to a canonical code (start from VeNom, so there is no taxonomy to defend). (2) Extract each policy form's exclusions, limits and waiting periods into clause-anchored rules once per form, human-verified. (3) Re-adjudicate independently and return agree or disagree per claim with a clause citation, sorted into three queues: likely overpaid, likely wrongly denied, and duplicate or tampered (PDF metadata, font and amount forensics). (4) Produce a monthly exam-ready validation pack with sample testing, drift and complaint linkage, which is what examiners request under the bulletin. (5) Cross-carrier registry: carriers contribute only hashed fingerprints (clinic, date, total, pet identity hash, line hashes) and get match alerts. Price benchmarks appear only as informational flags. They become a reason to reduce a payment only where the policy form has reasonable-and-customary language and the carrier opts in.
mutants.why_now: NAIC's AI model bulletin has been adopted by 25 states plus DC as of July 2026, and a 12-state examiner evaluation-tool pilot runs through September 2026. Under it, insurers stay accountable for vendor model outputs, and 'we cannot see the model internals' is not accepted. Pet premiums grew about 19% in 2025 on 6.98M insured US pets, and carriers are racing to automation (Five Sigma at Odie, Lassie at about 60% automated). LLMs make clause extraction from policy forms and PDF invoice reading cheap enough for a two-person team.
mutants.revenue_model: Annual platform fee of $45k-$120k by claim volume (about $0.15-$0.30 per claim scored), including monthly exam-ready packs. Registry-only tier of $12-25k for small carriers and TPAs. Optional 15% contingency on documented overpayments prevented on contract-clear lines. Sales math, assuming a $350 average paid claim: a 200k-claim MGA pays about $70M a year in claims, so an $80k fee breaks even at about 0.11% of claim dollars. Month-12 target: 6 MGAs at $80k plus 6 registry-tier customers at $15k, roughly $570k ARR. The registry then extends to all US carriers at a per-lookup fee, an ISO-ClaimSearch-style utility for pets.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Regulation has turned automation from a cost saver into a liability, and the vendors selling automation are structurally unable to vouch for themselves, the way an accounting firm cannot audit its own consulting work. Independence is the product, and it is a budget line that exists (compliance, delegated-authority audits) rather than one that has to be invented. Duplicate and tamper detection is the only kind of edit that gets more valuable with every carrier that joins and never requires fighting a vet or a policyholder. State anti-fraud immunity statutes generally permit sharing suspected-fraud data with anti-fraud organizations, which makes a hashed registry lawful to seed on day one.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: map which MGAs and small carriers have publicly announced automation, and list the NAIC-bulletin states each writes in. Recruit an ex-claims QA manager as design partner. Days 7-21: build the clause extractor on 10 public policy forms and the invoice normalizer on about 500 sample invoices. Days 14-30: cold-approach 25 heads of claims and compliance with a free 'exam-readiness shadow audit' of 2,000 of their auto-approved claims from the last 90 days. The deliverable is a one-page count of overpaid lines, likely wrongful denials and duplicates. Convert the best results to a $25k, 90-day paid pilot. Success is 3 signed pilots by day 90 and a registry seeded by those pilots' fingerprints.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Five Sigma, Sirma, and Lassie's in-house engine are the thing being audited, so they cannot sell independent validation. Five Sigma also does not describe unbundling or benchmarks, and Sirma is a bespoke services shop. Trupanion is in-house and never a customer, and we do not target it. VetControl is German, built on the GOT statutory fee schedule, names no US customers, and cannot read US policy clauses. FairVet and Vet Receipt are consumer bill-checkers with thin data and no insurer audit trail. Verisk's ISO pet program covers policy forms and rating only, so it is a possible acquirer or channel rather than a rival today. VeNom and SNOMED-VET are inputs, so the moat is the clause-to-line rule corpus, the pooled fingerprint registry and examiner-accepted evidence packs. Avoiding price-based reductions removes the balance-bill risk that the parent's research flagged.

mutants.title: UK Vet Price Panel for Investors and Insurers
mutants.one_liner: The first normalized, ownership-linked, time-series panel of UK vet prices, built from the price lists the CMA now forces every practice to publish, and licensed as a data feed to equity and credit investors, pet insurers and independent-practice bodies.
mutants.customer: Three payers with different budgets. (1) Buy-side and sell-side analysts and credit or private-equity funds with exposure to listed and sponsor-owned vet consolidators (CVS Group, Pets at Home/Vets4Pets, IVC Evidensia, Medivet, VetPartners, Linnaeus). (2) Pricing, claims and panel-strategy heads at UK pet insurers and their reinsurers. (3) Independent-practice trade bodies such as FIVP, which need to benchmark independents against groups. The first buyer to target is the analyst covering CVS Group, because alt-data budgets are large and the purchase decision is one person.
mutants.problem: Consolidators keep local practice brands after acquisition, so almost no one can build a clean same-practice, before-and-after price series by owner. The CMA found consolidated practices had about 5% higher claim values and 9.2% higher prices within four years, but insurers, lenders and analysts still cannot track drift by group or postcode. Insurers hold itemised claim lines but no market panel to compare them to. Investors underwrite price-led same-store growth with anecdotes. The official RCVS comparison data will not reach approved third parties until late 2027.
mutants.solution: Crawl and normalize the published price lists monthly, keeping history. The CMA order requires 36 standard items across six patient categories (216 prices per practice), written estimates over GBP 500, itemised bills, and ownership disclosure. Map each practice to its ultimate owner using the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Deliver: (a) a monthly group-level price index and same-practice change series, (b) a practice-level API with postcode reference ranges, (c) an alert feed when a group re-prices a category. Extension beyond the 36 routine items: insurers contribute itemised estimate and invoice lines above GBP 500 in exchange for a discount, which extends the panel to orthopaedics, oncology and emergency work. Apply to become an RCVS approved third party the day that channel opens, so the RCVS feed becomes an input rather than a threat. US extension later from insurer-contributed claim lines.
mutants.why_now: The CMA's final report (March 2026) became an order with RCVS undertakings accepted on 22 September 2026. Large groups' first transparency duties start 23 December 2026, and smaller practices follow through 2027. RCVS's enhanced Find a Vet is due by 22 June 2027, with business data supply later in 2027 and sharing with third parties under restrictions. That gives a 9-12 month window in which a normalized, owner-linked panel from the start of publication is the only structured source, and history cannot be back-filled later. Cheap LLM extraction handles the mess of 5,000 differently formatted price pages.
mutants.revenue_model: Data licences. Investor feed at GBP 30-60k a year. Insurer and reinsurer feed at GBP 20-50k, with a 40-50% discount for contributing itemised claim lines. Trade-body and independent-practice benchmarking at GBP 5-15k. Month-12 target of about GBP 550-600k ARR from 8 funds at 45k, 6 insurers at 30k and 3 bodies at 15k. Marginal cost is close to zero after the crawler exists. Year-2 upside comes from extending to US insurers' claim lines (US premiums grew about 19% in 2025) and to dental and specialty procedures.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The CMA did not only mandate price disclosure. It mandated ownership disclosure, and that is the join key nobody had. A price series linked to owner is worth far more to an investor than a price list is to a pet owner, so the buyer with the deepest pocket is not the insurer or the consumer. The panel is also a cornered resource in time: every month a rival waits is history they can never buy. The parent's canonical-code thesis still holds, because regulation just created the first common procedure list and this business maps to it before anyone else. Insurers' claim lines then extend that list into severity territory that the 36 routine items cannot reach.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: build crawlers for the six largest groups' price pages and 300 independents, and load the 36-item by six-category schema. Many practices already publish some prices ahead of the deadline. Days 10-20: build the ownership graph from the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Publish a free Pre-Order Baseline note on group price levels to draw inbound from analysts and journalists. Days 20-30: pitch 15 named buyers (5 analysts covering CVS Group and Pets at Home, 5 credit or PE funds with vet exposure, 5 insurer pricing heads) on a founding-subscriber annual deal at GBP 24k with a price lock and input on the index. Target 3 signed letters of intent by day 60 and the first live index the week after 23 December 2026.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: FairVet and Vet Receipt are US consumer bill-upload tools with thin, crowd-sourced data and no ownership graph, and neither sells institutional time series. Vet Price Comparison (UK) is a consumer directory, and RCVS Find a Vet is by design a directory rather than a league table, arrives mid-2027 and later becomes an input. AAHA's fee reference is a US survey, not a price panel. VetControl is German invoice verification for insurers and does not do UK market panels. Verisk's pet program is US policy and rating only. Trupanion and Lassie are in-house insurers and not customers, and UK insurers could scrape themselves but lack the cross-group history, the ownership join and neutral positioning. Selling to investors avoids the parent's balance-bill and vet-fight risk entirely, and the price index never reduces a policyholder's claim.

mutants.title: Pet Claims Clearinghouse Starting at the Front Desk
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of insurers policing vet invoices after the fact, give vet clinics a carrier-agnostic estimate-to-payout tool at the counter, then grow it into the standard transaction layer for pet insurance and a same-day payment network.
mutants.customer: Practice managers and lead client-service staff at independent and small-group US general-practice clinics (2-8 vets), and emergency or specialty hospitals where tickets run above $1,500. There are about 28,000 US vet hospitals. Later payers are pet insurers (per clean claim) and financing partners (per referred loan).
mutants.problem: An owner stands at the counter with a $3,800 estimate and says 'I have insurance'. It is one of about 15 carriers, the front desk cannot tell what will be covered, and the owner declines, delays, goes on credit or, in the worst case, euthanizes. Survey data shows 85% of vet professionals see owners decline recommended care at $1,000 or less, and they estimate about 13% of euthanasia decisions are driven by cost. After treatment, staff spend up to 30 minutes per claim in each insurer's own portal. Trupanion's VetDirect Pay shows clinics adopt this when it removes paperwork and lets them quote net of insurance (about 11,500 clinics as of October 2025, and a Digitail integration in August 2026), but it works only for Trupanion pets. Trupanion holds roughly 12% share in the market estimates found, so most insured pets have no such tool.
mutants.solution: Wedge product (shippable in about 10 weeks). Estimate Check: the front desk uploads the estimate or PMS export and the owner's policy PDF or insurance card. The tool returns per-line 'likely covered, likely excluded, needs records', a projected reimbursement range, and a one-page owner sheet showing what they will likely pay today and after reimbursement, with a financing option for any gap. It also shows the parent's edit logic turned around as provider-side scrubber tips ('these five lines are usually treated as included in the surgical fee; quote as a package price'). Claim Pack: after treatment it assembles the canonical invoice, records and the insurer's form, sends it through that insurer's intake channel, and tracks status. Network path: every estimate and reimbursement outcome trains per-insurer payout predictions. A published open transaction set (estimate, eligibility, claim, remittance on VeNom-based codes) is offered to insurers, who adopt it to cut intake cost. Later, an instant advance to clinics on insurer remits, funded by a warehouse line, turns it into a balance-sheet payment network.
mutants.why_now: Direct-pay proved clinic demand, but it is fragmented by carrier: Digitail and Trupanion announced their integration only in August 2026, and each new PMS-insurer pair is a one-off build. Insured pets are growing about 9% a year on a 4.27% penetration base, so the share of clinic estimates touched by insurance keeps rising. LLMs can now read arbitrary policy PDFs and messy estimates, which is what previously made a multi-carrier tool uneconomic. Corporate consolidation and price inflation make estimate conversations harder every quarter.
mutants.revenue_model: Phase 1: $199 a month per clinic location, sold on saved staff hours and higher treatment-plan acceptance, with a first-month free trial. Phase 2: insurers pay $0.75-$1.50 per clean canonical claim (their manual intake cost, an assumption to test), and financing partners pay a referral fee on loans originated at the estimate moment. Phase 3: 1.5-2.5% on advanced remit dollars (assumed range). Illustrative year-5 scale: 3,000 clinics at $2.4k is about $7M, 5M claims at $1 is about $5M, and $1B of advanced remits at 2% is about $20M, so roughly $30M of revenue on about a quarter of an estimated $4B of US claims paid.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: In human health, most claim edits run on the provider side, in clearinghouse scrubbers, before submission. Edits create value when they change behavior before the service, not when they reduce a payment afterwards. In pet insurance the only party who can renegotiate an estimate is the vet at the counter, and the only party with a real incentive at that moment is the clinic, because declined treatment is lost revenue. Flipping the parent's edits to the provider side removes its central risk (balance bills without vet contracts) and makes the vet a voluntary distribution channel. Whoever owns the estimate screen owns the transaction standard, just as the claim form did in human health, and the standard is worth more than any single edit library.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1-2: recruit an ex-practice-manager co-founder and sit with 10 clinics, shadowing 30 insured-estimate conversations. Collect 200 real estimates with matching policy documents and reimbursement outcomes from 5 friendly clinics. Week 2-3: build the line normalizer and coverage rules for the top 8 carriers from public policy forms. Week 3-4: run a manual-assist 'Estimate Check in 15 minutes' service for 10 clinics by text or email, free, and score predictions against actual reimbursements (target: within 10% of the actual payout on at least 70% of cases). Convert 5 clinics to $199 a month by day 30 and ask the two most engaged to introduce their PMS account manager, which starts the marketplace-app conversation.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Trupanion VetDirect Pay is single-carrier and proprietary, and it locks in Trupanion pets, so it cannot be the neutral rail, and the roughly 88% of the market outside its share is untouched by it. Insurer-specific direct-pay programs (Pets Best, ASPCA, Healthy Paws, PumpkinNow) each require a separate clinic workflow. PMS vendors (Digitail, Covetrus, IDEXX and others) integrate one insurer at a time, lack the insurer-side coverage logic, and are channel partners here rather than rivals. Five Sigma, Sirma, VetControl and Lassie sit on the insurer side and never see the estimate. FairVet and Vet Receipt are consumer after-the-fact bill checkers with no payout logic. Verisk standardized policy forms, not transactions. General eligibility-verification vendors (DoctorConnect lists pet insurers among its payers) are appointment and human-health tools without line-level pet estimates or claim packaging. I could not verify their depth, so that is a risk to test in the first 30 days. Moving the edits to the provider side also sidesteps the balance-bill and regulatory pushback the parent's research flagged.

mutants.title: AP-Inbox Implant Reconciler for Spine ASCs
mutants.one_liner: Forward your implant vendor invoices to one email address. We match each to the surgery, the payer's carve-out clause and the 835, and reopen the claim the day the invoice lands, so implant cost stops going unpaid.
mutants.customer: Independent, surgeon-owned spine and pain-management (spinal cord stimulator) ASCs doing about 100-600 implant cases a year. They have a one-to-three-person in-house billing office, or an outsourced biller paid a percentage of collections, and no supply-chain analyst. The buyer is the administrator plus the surgeon-owner who signs off on distributions. Launch in one state through its ASC association so outreach is dense.
mutants.problem: The leak is not ignorance of carve-outs (Becker's has covered them since 2014). It is a hand-off race. The claim leaves billing days after surgery. The consignment vendor invoice lands in accounts payable weeks later, if it is ever tied to the case. Sticker-sheet lot numbers, invoice lines and payer attachment rules share no common ID. So the claim goes out at charges, posts as 'paid', and no system emits the event 'invoice arrived for a case already billed'. Corrected-claim and appeal windows then expire silently. Testable hypothesis for the first audits: a meaningful share of implant cases have a claim date earlier than the invoice date. Each miss is worth roughly $5k-30k, and Medicare ASC cases are excluded because they are not carved out.
mutants.solution: (1) Zero-integration intake. Vendor invoices are auto-forwarded from the AP inbox, QuickBooks or Bill.com. An LLM extracts line items (manufacturer, catalog, lot, UDI-DI, unit price). The case schedule or implant log comes as a CSV or photos of sticker sheets, and the ERAs are pulled from the clearinghouse. No EHR or practice-management integration. (2) Rule engine with a payer-clause library. Contract PDFs are LLM-extracted and human-verified once, then reused across every ASC with the same payer. For workers' comp and no-fault, the engine uses public state fee schedules, several of which pay implants at invoice cost plus a capped markup (verify per state). This removes the 'read every contract' scaling limit. (3) The trigger. When an invoice matches a case already billed at $0 or bundled, it auto-builds the payer-specific attachment packet and corrected claim or appeal, ranked by days left to timely filing. Coders file for the first year, then automation. (4) A weekly one-page 'implant cash gap' for the administrator: unmatched invoices, invoice lag by vendor, payers paying $0.
mutants.why_now: ASC volume is shifting toward device-heavy musculoskeletal cases. CMS's CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) is reported to add more of them; verify the exact list. Becker's ran 'ASCs' implant cost problem' in March 2026 and 'payer terms ASCs can't miss' in July 2026. Payer AI payment-integrity tools now auto-zero claims that lack attachments. LLM invoice extraction, which used to need OCR templates per vendor, is now cents per invoice.
mutants.revenue_model: Lookback: 25% of cash actually collected on recovered carve-outs, over a 12-18 month lookback bounded by timely filing, with no fee if nothing is recovered. Then convert to $1.5-2.5k/month per ASC (or about $12 per implant case) for the invoice trigger and weekly digest. Hypothesis to prove in the audits: a 300-implant-case ASC with a 10% leak at about $8k a case is $240k a year, so about $60k of first-year contingency and $18-30k a year of recurring revenue. Fifty ASCs would be roughly $1M+ of ARR plus about $3M of one-time contingency.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The missing thing is an event, not data. Every RCM tool is triggered from the billing side, and nothing in the stack fires when an invoice arrives in AP after the claim is gone. Accounts payable is also the cheapest integration surface in healthcare, since forwarding email needs no IT project, so time-to-first-dollar is days. The wedge also counter-positions against billers. A percentage-of-collections biller cannot sell 'your billing is incomplete' without indicting itself, and the AP-side product never asks to replace them.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: DM or call 40 spine/SCS ASC administrators and surgeon-owners in one state via its ASC association and LinkedIn, offering a free 12-month lookback at 25% of cash collected only. Sign 3 design partners with a BAA. Week 2: pull 12 months of 835s, case and implant logs, and the AP invoice folder. Extract invoices with an LLM and spot-check to at least 95% line accuracy. Hand-read each site's top 3 commercial carve-out clauses. Week 3: match and measure three things. These are the share of implant cases where the claim predates the invoice, the implant lines paid $0 or bundled where the clause says carve-out, and the dollars still inside timely filing. Week 4: file the first 15-25 corrected claims and appeals, write a one-page anonymized leak report, and start outbound to 40 more ASCs. Gate: continue only if at least 2 of 3 sites show identifiable, collectible leakage of at least 3% of implant spend. Otherwise narrow to newly opened or converted ASCs, or kill.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Aspirion (ContractIQ), FinThrive Contract Manager, Sift RevProtect, Waystar and MDaudit all start from claims and contract models sold to hospital revenue-cycle teams. None ingest vendor AP invoices or fire on invoice arrival, and they are retrospective variance tools, not per-case attachment and corrected-claim builders. This product is sold to the ASC owner and administrator as a supply-chain-to-cash control, which those enterprise sellers do not reach. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways sit in the practice-management and billing workflow that this product deliberately stays outside, so it works with any biller or PM system. Defensibility comes from the cross-ASC payer-clause library and invoice-lag dataset, which is a cornered resource, and from the switching cost of becoming the ASC's implant ledger. If Aspirion bolts on contract-level carve-outs, it still needs the AP-side intake and the ASC-owner sale.

mutants.title: Carve-Out Audit Kit for Challenger ASC Billers
mutants.one_liner: A white-label implant carve-out engine for independent ASC billing companies, who use a free lookback on a prospect or new client as their sales weapon and split the recovered dollars with us.
mutants.customer: Independent ASC billing and RCM companies with roughly 8-60 ASC clients. These are the long tail behind SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble. The buyer is the owner or head of sales. The ASC still pays the fee, but through its biller.
mutants.problem: Billers win ASC clients on percentage fee and references, and the new-ASC wave makes that fight harder. They can't afford implant analysts or invoice-parsing tooling for 30 clients. A startup selling direct to ASCs hits a trust wall, because owners won't hand 835s and contracts to an unknown vendor. Billers already hold the BAAs, the ERA feeds and the contract PDFs. Billers also don't buy 'recovery', because it admits past misses. They buy client acquisition and retention.
mutants.solution: White-label 'Carve-Out Desk' with three parts. (1) Lookback as an RFP weapon. For a prospect, or a new client in its first 30 days, ingest 12-24 months of 835s, implant log and AP invoices and return a co-branded Carve-Out Leak Report showing dollars by payer and CPT. The new biller can recover the prior biller's misses with no political cost. (2) Recovery ops. We prepare attachment packets and corrected claims and appeals, and the biller submits, or we do so under the biller's credentials. (3) A prospective pre-bill gate, delivered as upload plus a review queue that works with whichever PM system the biller's clients use, checking invoice attached and L8699/027x coded to trigger the carve-out. Each partner audit adds payer-clause entries to a shared clause library.
mutants.why_now: New and converting spine and ortho ASCs are choosing billers now, as CMS's CY2026 ASC rule (CMS-1834-FC) reportedly expands the ASC list; verify the exact list. Payer AI payment integrity makes attachment mistakes costly. Invoice parsing now costs cents, so the audit can be run for a prospect who has not yet signed. Becker's coverage in 2026 shows implant cost is the hot ASC topic, so billers have a live sales angle.
mutants.revenue_model: Money flow: the payer pays the ASC as usual. The ASC pays the biller 25-30% of recovered carve-out dollars under a 'Carve-Out Assurance' schedule the biller adds to its contract. The biller remits about 50-60% of that to us, so we take roughly 15% of recovered dollars and the biller keeps roughly 10-12% for near-zero labor. On top, $300-600 per facility per month for the pre-bill gate and a $2-4k flat fee per prospect lookback, credited against the rev-share. Illustrative unit economics, to be verified in pilots: a facility recovering $240k in year one yields about $36k to us plus about $6k of platform fees. Twenty partners with an average of 20 implant-heavy clients each is 400 facilities, which supports a $5-10M ARR outcome.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The biller's incentives are the opposite of the ASC's. Incumbents will not audit themselves, but their challengers desperately want a proof-of-value opener. The moment of highest willingness to pay is a biller switch or a new ASC opening, because the prior party's misses can be recovered with no blame. The channel also removes the hardest part of direct sales: data access and trust arrive through an existing BAA chain. Every partner lookback grows the cross-client clause library, and an incumbent biller who refuses the tool becomes exposed to challengers who use it.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a list of about 150-200 independent ASC billers from ASCA and state ASC association vendor directories, Becker's ASC sponsor lists and LinkedIn. Pitch 40 owners by phone with one offer: 'Give me one prospect you're pitching, or your newest client, and I'll return a co-branded carve-out leak report in 10 days, free.' Convert 3 pilots with 2 audits each, run by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet plus an LLM for invoices. Success: at least $100k of collectible carve-out dollars found on 2 of 3 audits, and one biller signing the rev-share and the Carve-Out Assurance add-on. Kill signal: billers say they already catch this and the reports show under 2% leakage. In that case pivot to selling direct to in-house-billing ASCs.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: It does not fight SIS/Surgical Notes, NMBS or Nimble head-on. It sells to their challengers and gives them a weapon the incumbents' scale doesn't cover. Aspirion, FinThrive, Sift and Waystar are enterprise tools for health systems and contingency recoverers that would compete with billers on recovery, so billers won't buy or partner with them. Aspirion could add carve-outs, but it would sell to ASCs directly and cannot use a biller channel without cannibalizing its own contingency model. HST Pathways and SIS software hold the inventory data but are tied to their own PM platforms, while this kit is PM-agnostic, and they can be data sources rather than rivals. Defensibility comes from the shared payer-clause library and from switching costs once a biller's sales deck and onboarding process depend on the leak report.

mutants.title: Implant Payment Index for ASC Networks
mutants.one_liner: Pool invoice-versus-payment data across physician-owned ASC networks to build the payer-by-procedure benchmark that only payers hold today, and turn it into the reference price index that carve-out contracts cite instead of each ASC's own invoice.
mutants.customer: First buyers are ASC management companies, physician-owned ASC networks of 5-40 centers, and state ASC associations, all facing payer contract renewals. Later buyers are ASC developers, lenders and PE sponsors building pro formas, and eventually payers licensing the index.
mutants.problem: Every carve-out claim hands the payer the vendor invoice, so payers hold the largest SKU-level implant price database in the country and use it in contract talks. Becker's July 2026 reported that this year's payer talks came down to fine print, implant costs and case-level cost data. ASCs' invoices are trapped in AP, so each ASC negotiates knowing only its own numbers. Drugs have a public ASP benchmark, while devices have none, so carve-outs reference each ASC's invoice. Payers distrust that (invoice inflation, related-party distributors) and demand attachments, which creates the paperwork and the leak in the parent idea.
mutants.solution: Wedge product: the Payer Implant Scorecard. From de-identified 835s, case lists and a sample of invoices, per payer and CPT it reports the share of implant lines paid $0, realized payment as a ratio of invoice cost, markup actually realized versus the clause, and how the network's terms compare with peer networks. It ends in a negotiation memo with the dollar impact of each ask. Data is contributed give-to-get, and contributors also get a free carve-out lookback that feeds the recovery business. Governance: cells need at least 5 contributors, data lags at least 90 days, nothing is forward-looking, and outputs are ratios rather than vendor prices, with antitrust counsel reviewing the protocol. Then a quarterly published Implant Reference Index and a Model Carve-Out Clause (index plus X%, no per-claim invoice attachment). Later modules include developer and lender pro formas by payer mix and, eventually, a payer license.
mutants.why_now: Implant cost is the central ASC economics story of 2026 (Becker's, March and July 2026). Volume is moving to ASCs as CMS's CY2026 rule reportedly expands the ASC covered list; verify the exact list. Payers are using AI payment-integrity tools that will only get stricter on attachments, which gives them a reason to want an index. Invoice and contract extraction is cheap enough to build the dataset without armies of coders.
mutants.revenue_model: Networks pay $25-60k a year, or about $2-4k a facility a month, for the scorecard and quarterly refresh, plus a success fee of 10% of the first 24 months of measured implant reimbursement uplift after a renegotiation, measured on the same 835s. Data and pro forma licenses to developers, lenders and sponsors are later. A payer index license comes only once the index is a contract reference. Bottom-up: about 1,000-1,200 implant-heavy physician-owned ASCs at roughly $30k a year is $30-36M before the index and lender products.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The information asymmetry runs in the opposite direction from what ASCs assume. Payers already hold the invoices, since ASCs have been sending them for years, but ASCs do not hold each other's. Because the deliverable is a ratio (paid divided by invoice cost) and not a price, it can be shared without breaching vendor price-confidentiality clauses. Once contracts reference the index, both sides drop the per-claim attachment process that causes the leak. A neutral index is also something an ASC-billing company or PM vendor cannot publish, since it would expose their own clients' leaks and their customers' data-sharing limits.
mutants.first_30_days: Recruit 3 ASC networks or MSOs plus one state ASC association, preferring those with payer renewals in the next 6 months. Week 1: offer a free 'zero-pay scan' that needs only 835s and a case list, showing the share of implant lines (L8699, 027x, C-codes) paid $0 by payer and CPT. Week 2: engage antitrust and health-privacy counsel to sign off on the data protocol and BAA/de-identification. Week 3: for the first network, add 20-30 invoices per top payer and CPT to convert zero-pay rates into dollars. Week 4: deliver the first Scorecard and negotiation memo for a live renewal, and sell a paid $15-25k pilot to two more networks. Kill signal: no network will pool data even under the protocol, or scan results show payers already pay implants at cost-plus almost everywhere.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Aspirion ContractIQ, FinThrive Contract Manager and Sift model one provider's contracts against its own claims. None pool implant invoice-to-payment data across many ASCs, and their buyer is hospital revenue-cycle staff, not ASC networks negotiating renewals. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways hold multi-ASC data, but as PM and billing vendors they lack AP invoices and contract clauses, and their incentives don't favor benchmarks that show client leaks. Consultants use anecdote and fee schedules. The moat is network economics plus a cornered dataset, and standard-setting via the model clause and index. Waystar, MDaudit and Aspirion sell workflow and recovery, and none of them are positioned to become a neutral price reference.

mutants.title: Mixed-Lot Calf Referee With Brix Price Formulas
mutants.one_liner: An independent, photo-stamped Brix grade taken at the broker's loading dock that turns a blind mixed-dairy calf lot into a formula-priced lot, so the best dairies stop subsidizing the worst and disputes get settled by schedule, not argument.
mutants.customer: Wedge: independent calf brokers and sale-barn aggregators who assemble roughly 200-800 day 2-7 beef-on-dairy calves a week from 10-30 dairies and sell them to raisers who have no history with any of the source dairies. Start with 3-5 brokers in one dairy-dense region. Second payer: the raisers who buy those lots. Not the target: contracted dairy-to-ranch flows and integrated operators, where source reputation already does the job.
mutants.problem: Mixed-source lots are priced at a lemons discount. The buyer cannot tell which dairy's calves are good, so he pays for the average and hedges for the worst, and good dairies subsidize bad ones. Brokers eat 'adjustments' and lose a buyer after one bad lot. When calves die at the raiser, the dispute cannot be resolved: the dairy blames luck and the raiser blames the calves. A raiser can self-test for $1, but the seller will not accept the buyer's number, and the buyer will not accept the seller's, so measurement alone settles nothing. Packers already apply standardized deductions for unknown health history, so that discount is passed back upstream to brokers.
mutants.solution: 1) Two techs sample at unload or loading: every calf in lots sold as 'graded', a 20-calf random sample in standard lots. One phone frame captures ear tag, tube label and the refractometer display, timestamped and geotagged, so custody is the product. 2) Each calf is graded on the Lombard four-tier scale and the lot gets a score. 3) The lot quote carries a pre-agreed Settlement Schedule: a price add per Excellent/Good head, and an automatic per-head credit if Poor exceeds an agreed share of the lot (for example 30%). The buyer accepts or rejects at arrival by formula. This is a price term, not insurance or a warranty. 4) The broker uses the grades to split lots by dairy quality and sell the top tier at a spread. 5) The referee also holds the tag-level chain of custody for any 30-day death dispute (necropsy photo plus treatment log).
mutants.why_now: Crossbred calves at $1,000-1,500 make a 10-point mortality gap worth $100+ a head, so the number now matters to a broker's P&L. Feeders are being told not to assume a crossbred premium, so the market's question is shifting from 'what genetics' to 'which calves live'. The Lombard 2020 four-tier standard exists, digital refractometers cost about $150, and photo-stamped custody capture on a phone is now trivial to build. The same lot could not have been priced this way in 2019, when a calf was worth a fraction as much.
mutants.revenue_model: $5 per graded calf, split between broker and buyer. In the first 90 days, success-based: the fee is due only on lots that clear at least $10 a head over the ungraded quote, so grading pays for itself before it bills. Add $75 per settlement or claim adjudication and a $250/month broker dashboard with a dairy league table. Honest sizing: 300 calves a week per broker is about $78K a year, so 15 brokers is about $1.2M. Test fees alone cap out in the low millions, so the wedge's real value is the custody dataset, which is the base for the guarantee and warranty layers in the other branches.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The product is not the number, it is the pre-agreed price formula attached to it. Disclosure unravels (Grossman-Milgrom): once the two or three best dairies in a lot prove Excellent, any dairy that refuses grading gets priced as Poor, so you only have to win the best sellers rather than the whole market. And no buyer needs to state a premium: the money is the lemons discount already being taken out of good calves in mixed lots, which sidesteps the 'no proven crossbred premium' headwind.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: recruit one broker or sale barn moving 300+ calves a week, and pick their 3 best dairies (the ones who want to prove it). Buy two refractometers, tubes and centrifuge or clot rack, and set up a photo-stamp capture form on a no-code tool. Weeks 2-4: grade every calf free at loading (about 1,200 calves), send lot sheets and a proposed Settlement Schedule to 2-3 buyers, and ask them to report 30-day illness and death by ear tag. Day 45 go/no-go gates: (a) at least one buyer signs a schedule with a spread of $25 or more a head between Good-or-better and Poor; (b) Poor calves show at least 1.5x the 30-day loss of Excellent/Good. If either fails, stop. Before spending on anything else, verify the 10-25% raiser-loss figure from the parent, since it is unsourced.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Where Food Comes From audits marketing claims (age, source, process) on a program basis; this sells per-lot physical sampling and a pricing formula at the moment of sale, and could give WFCF a certificate to resell as a Process Verified module instead of competing with it. Calftech-style integrated ranches keep data in-house because they own both sides; this only sells into unintegrated trade (mixed lots), and an integrated operator buying outside calves becomes a customer. The $1 self-test objection is answered because the product removes the need to trust the other party, not the need to measure. Bilateral-history substitution is avoided by targeting only lots where no history exists. Warranty moral hazard is avoided because nothing here insures the raiser's management.

mutants.title: Lender-Paid Calf Collateral Inspection and Lot Grading
mutants.one_liner: Sell independent day-3-to-6 lot grading to the feed, milk-replacer and ag-loan credit desks that finance calf raisers, as collateral inspection, so the party who really loses money on every dead calf pays for the measurement.
mutants.customer: Credit managers at regional feed and milk-replacer distributors that carry 30-90 day trade credit to calf ranches, and ag lenders and calf-ownership financing programs that lend against calf inventory. Wedge: one distributor with 15-40 non-integrated calf-raiser accounts and $2M or more in calf-related receivables. Raisers are the secondary beneficiary and pay through a loan-document inspection fee or through better credit terms.
mutants.problem: A 500-head lot of crossbred calves is now $500-750K of collateral, and the lender's monitoring is still a headcount and the raiser's own say-so. A bad intake lot with poor passive transfer can lose a large share of its calves within weeks (the parent's 10-25% raiser loss is unverified). My inference, to be validated in customer calls, is that the credit desk usually learns of it from a missed payment 30-60 days later. The lender cannot trust the raiser's self-reported Brix, and the raiser cannot prove to the lender that a bad lot was bad luck at intake rather than bad management. Nobody prices the biological quality of the collateral.
mutants.solution: For each new lot placed at a financed ranch, an independent tech samples 20 calves within 24-72 hours of arrival (day 3-6 of age), with custody-stamped tube and tag capture. Within 24 hours the credit desk receives a Lot Risk Grade (A-D) built from the Lombard tiers, with an expected 30-day loss band, taken from the published roughly 2x risk for failure of passive transfer at first and replaced by our own pooled data. Credit terms key off the grade: A lots get full limit and fast approval, C/D lots trigger a hold or a risk-sharing plan. The raiser gets a same-day early-warning call for D lots (isolate Poor calves, fluid and treatment protocol), so the inspection is a service to them rather than a tax. Year 2: a loss-outcome dataset licensed to reinsurers and MGAs.
mutants.why_now: Crossbred calf collateral per head has multiplied several times over versus a few years ago (beef-on-dairy went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to about 3.2M in 2024 per the parent, and calves have reached $1,500), so headcount-style monitoring that was fine at $100 a calf is negligent at $1,400. Cheap refractometers, phone custody capture and now a published grading standard make lot inspection cost about $1.50-2 a calf. The 2020 consensus tiers give lenders a common language for the first time.
mutants.revenue_model: $250-450 per lot inspected (about $1.50-2 per calf), billed to the lender or supplier and recoverable from the raiser as a collateral inspection fee, plus $150-300 a month per financed ranch for the monitoring dashboard. A ranch placing 300 calves a week is about 52 lots a year, or roughly $18K a year. A distributor with 40 accounts is about $700K a year. Later: loss-data license to insurers and reinsurers, and a per-lot fee for a lender-requested claims audit. Market ceiling on fees is modest but recurring, and the buyer's value (bad debt avoided) is a multiple of the fee.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The party with the most money at risk per dead calf is not in the room and is not the raiser. It is the credit provider. Collateral management (independent inspectors working for banks) is an old, boring industry that has never priced the biological quality of livestock. This makes the business independent of two weaknesses in the parent: it needs no buyer premium for graded calves, and it avoids warranty moral hazard because the customer prices and monitors credit rather than insuring loss.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-14: hold 20 short calls with credit managers at feed and milk-replacer distributors and ag loan officers in one dairy-dense county. Ask what they lose per year to calf-ranch defaults, how they learn of a bad lot, and whether collateral inspection fees are already collectible under their loan documents. Days 15-30: sign a free 60-day pilot with one distributor covering 6 friendly ranches. Two techs, about 12 lots a week, and a 24-hour grade report the credit manager marks up with what they would have changed. At day 60, compare grade against 30-day loss and any past-due behavior, then ask for a signed $300-a-lot agreement. Gate: the credit manager names annual avoided bad debt of at least 10x the annual fee. If lenders will not state a number, kill it. Before pitching, verify the loss-rate and market-size figures and check for existing livestock collateral inspection firms.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Where Food Comes From sells claim verification to marketers, brands and packers. It has no lender product and does no per-lot sampling for credit decisions, so the buyer and the job are different. Calftech-style integrated ranches self-fund and self-monitor, so they are out of scope by design. This targets non-integrated raisers who have to prove intake quality to a lender, and independence is what makes an inspection valid collateral evidence. The $1 self-test objection disappears, because the lender is exactly the party who cannot accept the raiser's own test. There is no dependence on a graded-calf premium (the parent's weakest evidence) and no underwriting exposure. Vets who already test at herd checks work for the raiser and cannot serve as the lender's independent eyes.

mutants.title: Dairy-Backed Calf Guarantee Pool With Immune Screening
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of selling buyers a verification and later insuring the raiser, make the dairy, who controls colostrum, warrant its own graded calves for 21 days, with our grade as the price of admission and a reserve pool we administer, growing into a mutual or captive with an MGA and reinsurer behind it.
mutants.customer: Large dairies (roughly 1,000+ cows, which now sell hundreds to a couple thousand crossbred calves a year, a $0.5-2M line that they still treat as a sideline) that already run good colostrum programs (pasteurized colostrum, Brix testing) and are irritated at being priced at the herd average. First: 3-5 dairies in one region. Second payer: the raisers who pay a premium for guaranteed calves. Later: an insurer or MGA taking over the pool's tail risk.
mutants.problem: A dairy with excellent colostrum management cannot credibly say so, so it gets the average price. Buyers cannot underwrite the calves, and insurers cannot underwrite a raiser's loss because the raiser's housing and feeding confound the cause of death (the parent's own moral hazard problem), and federal Livestock Risk Protection excludes mortality and disease. Both sides distrust each other's numbers, and the grade alone still leaves the raiser holding the risk. The dairy owns the biggest early-death driver and holds none of the downside.
mutants.solution: Each enrolled dairy has every calf graded at day 3-5 by us. Excellent and Good calves get a Guaranteed tag: if a calf dies of covered causes (neonatal scours, sepsis, weak-calf, navel) within 21 days of delivery, the buyer gets a replacement or price credit up to the lot price. Claims are adjudicated by us using tag custody, necropsy photos or vet note and treatment log within 72 hours. Trauma and raiser-negligence exclusions plus a small buyer co-pay keep the raiser's incentives in play. The dairy pays a per-calf assessment into a segregated reserve we administer, priced by grade and falling as the dairy's grade mix improves, so fixing colostrum is directly rewarded. Poor calves are sold openly at a discount without a guarantee. Unused reserve is rebated at year end, mutual style. Stage 2 (about 50,000 graded calves): a licensed MGA with a fronting carrier and stop-loss reinsurance. Stage 3: a risk retention group or captive owned by participating dairies.
mutants.why_now: Beef-on-dairy volume is heading from about 3.2M toward the 5-6M CattleFax projects, at four-figure prices, so a dairy's calf revenue is finally large enough to fund a guarantee and its reputation is worth protecting. A published four-tier standard gives a shared, auditable eligibility rule. Packers already penalize unknown health history and the heifer shortage makes each lost calf expensive to replace, so buyers want risk transfer more than they want a certificate. Cheap custody capture makes claims adjudicable at a few dollars per claim.
mutants.revenue_model: $5 per graded calf plus 15-25% administration and commission on guarantee assessments (assessments of about $15-30 per guaranteed calf, in line with an expected covered-loss cost near $15-20 on a $1,200 calf at 1.5% early loss, to be checked against real data), plus profit commission from the reinsurer and float on reserves. Dairy economics: a $35-60 buyer premium against a $15-30 assessment, so about $15-25 net per calf. On 1,000 calves that is a modest but real $15-25K a year. Mature sizing: 500K guaranteed calves a year is about $5M in fees and commissions, with a $10-30M revenue ceiling at 1-2M calves, if the pool becomes the industry standard. The moat is the dataset, the escrow role and the mutual's membership, not the refractometer.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is the cheapest credible signal there is (Spence): a seller who will pay if the calf dies proves quality without the buyer trusting any measurement. It also flips the moral hazard. In the first 21 days the risk is controlled by the party paying for it, the dairy, which is why insuring the raiser is hard and warranting the dairy's calves is not. The grade becomes the actuarial rate table rather than a label, and dairies with bad colostrum programs are priced out until they fix them, which turns a data business into a compliance flywheel.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-14: sign 3-5 large dairies with pasteurized colostrum programs, plus one raiser or broker who will state a premium for guaranteed calves. Draft a one-page 21-day replacement-credit warranty (covered causes, exclusions, 72-hour claim rule, cap at lot price) and get it reviewed by an ag attorney, since a seller's own warranty is a sale-of-goods term but pooling across sellers may be insurance under state law. Open an escrow account. Days 15-30: grade and guarantee a 1,000-calf pilot with each dairy prefunding a $20 per calf reserve. Run the 21-day window and publish the claims ratio. Gates: claims under 80% of assessments and the buyer pays $35 or more a head over the ungraded price. If claims are high, reprice or drop the dairy. Stage 2 only after 50,000 graded calves and a signed MGA term sheet.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Where Food Comes From is a verifier and does not take underwriting positions or hold per-calf outcome data, so it can be a claims-audit partner rather than a rival. Calftech-style integrated ranches earn credibility by owning both ends and keeping data in-house. This gives any dairy the same credibility without owning a ranch, as a capital-light replica of vertical integration, and integrated operators simply become additional buyers of guaranteed calves. The parent's stated obstacles are answered directly. Self-testing is irrelevant because the guarantee, not the number, carries the trust. Bilateral history is replaced by a financial commitment. Warranty moral hazard is contained by a short window on dairy-controlled causes, exclusions and a co-pay. No federal mortality cover exists (LRP excludes it), and I could not verify what private livestock mortality insurance exists, so the plan partners with an MGA instead of competing with one.

mutants.title: Dual-Mode Genset Permits for Queued Campuses
mutants.one_liner: Design the air permit for new data center campuses before the generators are bought, so the backup fleet is legally curtailment-ready from day one and the fee is tied to energization date.
mutants.customer: Energy and development leads at spec developers, powered-shell builders and neocloud/colo operators with 50-400 MW campuses in PJM (AEP Ohio, Dominion, ComEd, PPL). The wedge is campuses that have filed, or are about to file, their air-permit application and have not yet placed genset purchase orders. Hyperscalers with in-house permitting teams are excluded at first. Air consultants are a secondary channel.
mutants.problem: The parent's real cost is retrofitting existing Tier 2 emergency fleets. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), emergency engines are capped at 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of that can earn income or serve a financial arrangement. Reclassifying an installed fleet means stricter engine standards, re-permitting and public comment. Yet the largest cohort of new engines is being permitted right now as emergency-only, because that is the cheapest and fastest path. That choice locks out capacity and curtailment use for 15 or more years. PJM's curtail-or-bring-capacity direction means those same campuses will need on-site backup to energize earlier. Nobody is designing the permit for that second use at the moment the choice is cheap.
mutants.solution: A fixed-price 'Dual-Mode Permit Package' sold before genset purchase orders and inside the air-permit comment window. (1) A one-time state legal feasibility memo from a retained air attorney (VA, OH, IL, PA), which gates every engagement. (2) An engine spec that is Tier 4 Final or SCR-ready, with catalyst and urea footprint reserved, ECM hour-metering and paralleling ready. This turns retrofit financing into a spec change costing a fraction of a retrofit. (3) Permit application language and modeling: an emergency mode plus a capped grid-emergency/curtailment mode of roughly 100-200 hours, synthetic-minor NOx limits, 1-hour NO2 dispersion modeling, and a community disclosure plan. (4) A curtailment-readiness dossier the utility and PJM can cite when offering earlier or flexible energization. Engines are certified as non-emergency-capable from the start, so the campus never has to fight the emergency-to-non-emergency reclassification.
mutants.why_now: Turbines are sold out until roughly 2029-30, so the practical path to earlier energization is on-site capacity that can be built now. PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short, and the connect-and-manage and bring-your-own-capacity framework is being filed at FERC. Large OEM gensets with SCR options are catalog items, and campuses energizing in 2028-30 must order engines and file permits in the next 6-12 months. This would not have worked in 2019, when there was no curtailment penalty for missing on-site capacity.
mutants.revenue_model: $60-150k fixed fee per campus (feasibility memo, spec, permit drafting, modeling). A success fee applies when the permit issues with the dual-mode condition (about $50k), and a further one applies only when the utility or PJM offers earlier or flexible energization that cites the dossier, at roughly $1-2k per MW per month of acceleration. A 200 MW campus energized six months early is worth about $1-2M to us. A colo campus that size earns on the order of $30M a month at full lease-up, so the buyer's return is 50x or more. An optional 10% share of capacity revenue for five years is secondary. Illustrative unit economics: 10 campuses in year one is roughly $1.5-3M, with two lawyers, two engineers and one permit modeler.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The cheapest time to unlock diesel is before it exists. The permit design is a one-time, 15-year decision, and taking it at application costs a fraction of a retrofit. It turns the parent's hardest problem (retrofit financing plus reclassification risk) into a purchase-spec problem that the buyer is already paying for. It also changes what is being sold, from capacity revenue that the buyer discounts to time. Energization date is the metric a developer's CFO already tracks, and every month of delay costs more than any capacity payment. Public permit dockets show exactly which campuses are in the window, so lead generation is a scrape rather than cold outreach.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: commission the air-attorney feasibility memo ($8-10k), covering which engine and classification path works in VA, OH, IL and PA. If no path closes at Tier 4 or SCR cost, stop. Weeks 1-2: scrape VA DEQ, Ohio EPA, IEPA and PA DEP public notices for data center genset permit applications filed in the last 12 months (target 40) and identify the developer and the consultant of record for each. Weeks 2-4: cold-contact the development leads and offer a $12k 'dual-mode gap review' of the pending application inside the public comment window. In parallel, offer the applicants' air consultants a white-label subcontract for the dual-mode module. Aim for two paid gap reviews and one campus package LOI. The demand test is whether a developer will pay before PO to keep the option open.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Trinity-type consultancies sell reactive, hourly permit work, are not tied to capacity or energization outcomes, and do not spec engines. We offer them the dual-mode module as a white-label add-on rather than compete. Voltus and CPower can only enroll resources that are already dual-mode, so we are their upstream and never touch enrollment or the DR revenue relationship. ERock sells gas hardware and a bridge-to-grid story. We are engine-agnostic and ride on gensets the campus must buy anyway, so there is no incremental hardware capex to finance. We also avoid the parent's unproven retrofit-of-Tier-2 step and its legal trap by working only on greenfield permits, and we gate on the attorney memo.

mutants.title: Lender-Required Curtailment Reports for Data Centers
mutants.one_liner: An independent, productized report, like a Phase I environmental report but for power, that tells data center lenders how many hours a campus can legally run its generators when the grid curtails it.
mutants.customer: Debt originators, underwriters and portfolio managers who finance data centers where the lender carries power risk directly: neocloud GPU-backed delayed-draw loans, spec and powered-land developers without an investment-grade tenant, and ABS/CMBS arrangers and rating analysts. The borrower pays at closing, as it already does for lender-required third-party reports. Independent engineers and lender counsel are the channel. Start with PJM and ERCOT campuses.
mutants.problem: Every underwriting model assumes that if PJM or ERCOT curtails the campus, the on-site generators cover it. Federal engine rules and state air permits cap those engines at roughly 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of it can be run for money or under a financial arrangement. Texas SB 6 even states that it does not authorize violating emissions limits. A campus curtailed for 200 hours can be legally uncovered after 100. Lenders have no independent way to check this. The operator's own consultant is conflicted, and independent engineers are generalists. The exposure is real but unquantified, and it will be priced once someone quantifies it.
mutants.solution: A standardized 'Curtailment Runway Report', delivered in about five business days. It has four parts. (1) The permit-derived legal runway: per-engine hour caps, engine tier, allowed uses, monitoring and reporting duties, and remaining headroom. (2) Operational runway: fuel on site, paralleling and telemetry status, and the test and maintenance hours already consumed. (3) A curtailment-exposure distribution for the campus's utility and market zone. (4) A cost-to-cure estimate (permit modification, SCR, hour cap changes). Every report cites the permit conditions it relies on and is reviewed by a retained air attorney. A portfolio subscription adds permit-change alerts and annual surveillance refreshes. Campuses that score badly become inbound leads for the sharpened dual-mode permit service.
