mutants.why_now: PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short and its board plan lets large loads bring their own capacity or accept earlier curtailment. The curtailment rules are now credit terms rather than a policy debate. Texas SB 6 requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose backup generation and lets ERCOT direct deployment, so disclosure data will exist for the first time. Data center financing volume is large and recurring, and power availability is now the top diligence item. LLM-assisted structuring of permit PDFs collapses the cost of producing a first-draft report, while attorney review keeps it defensible.
mutants.revenue_model: $20-45k per closing report, paid by the borrower through the lender's third-party report budget. Annual surveillance refresh at $8-12k per campus. Lender or rating-agency portfolio subscriptions at $150-400k a year for unlimited reports and change alerts. Illustrative sizing to validate: 150 financings a year x $30k, plus 400 refreshes x $8k, plus 10 subscriptions x $250k, is roughly $10M annual revenue. Gross margin is high once permits are structured, because the same permit dataset serves every report. A white-label channel to independent engineers is a second line.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The parent's permit dataset is worth more as a warning than as an unlock. Everyone else asks how much diesel can become capacity. The same facts show that the fallback everyone already assumes is often illegal past the cap, which is a downside risk with a faster buyer and no retrofit capex. Lenders reliably pay for independent third-party reports that gate a closing (Phase I environmental reports are the analogy, and the database company behind them proved the data business). Independence is the product. The operator's consultant cannot sell the same report, and aggregators profit from enrollment and have no incentive to say 'no'. A bad score also creates the demand the unlock business could never verify.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: build 10 sample reports on publicly permitted PJM and ERCOT campuses using permit files and disclosure data, and retain an air attorney to co-sign the methodology. Days 5-25: interview 15 people, namely data center debt originators, private credit underwriters, ABS/CMBS rating analysts, lender counsel and independent engineers, to find who owns power diligence in credit committee and which live deals are closing in the next 90 days. Days 20-30: offer three free reports on live deals in exchange for a 30-minute review and permission to cite, then price the fourth at $25k. Get one independent-engineer white-label LOI. The riskiest assumption is that a lender will make this a closing condition. Test it by asking for the condition in writing.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Voltus, CPower and ERock are sellers of megawatts, so they have no incentive to tell a lender a campus is uncovered, and none serves the capital-markets buyer. Trinity works for the operator, which is a conflict in a lender report, and it sells hourly permit projects rather than a standardized, comparable score. Independent engineers are the likely adjacent entrants. We sell to them white-label and win on speed, a permit-structured dataset and a lawyer-reviewed methodology. No competitor found in the parent's research sells to lenders, insurers or rating analysts.

mutants.title: Dispatch-Eligibility Registry for Backup Generators
mutants.one_liner: Become the neutral system of record for whether each backup generator may legally run for the grid right now, starting as a Texas SB 6 compliance product and growing into the rail that ERCOT, PJM, utilities and aggregators check before dispatch.
mutants.customer: First buyer: environmental and compliance leads at 75 MW+ data centers in Texas, who face the SB 6 disclosure and deploy-on-direction duty and must not violate emissions limits. Then PJM colos that must prove permit compliance to state air agencies and counties. Then DR aggregators, utilities and RTOs that consume the dispatch-eligibility certificate through an API. Later expansion is to hospitals, water utilities and telecom, where the wider standby generator fleet is far larger (widely cited estimates run into the hundreds of GW, which I have not verified).
mutants.problem: Backup generation is the largest idle block of capacity, but it can only be called if three things are true at the moment of the call: the engine is permitted for that use, it has hours left in the rolling year, and the trigger is a legally recognized emergency. Today the answer sits in permit PDFs, OEM dashboards and spreadsheets. Regulators cannot see it, so they say no. Aggregators carry enforcement risk and cannot prove compliance. Communities suspect the worst about diesel, which sinks permits. Nobody can be sure that dispatching an engine on a given day will not breach a cap.
mutants.solution: A run-hour ledger and certificate service. Step one is software only: an ingest of permit conditions (LLM-structured, attorney-reviewed) plus monthly or continuous hour-meter data from BMS exports, OEM telemetry or a read-only J1939/Modbus tap, with non-resettable meter attestation as a fallback. It computes remaining permitted hours per engine, tags every run with its legal basis (test, maintenance, emergency, directed deployment), auto-generates regulator deviation and compliance reports, and publishes a public disclosure page. Step two is a machine-readable Dispatch Eligibility Certificate (open schema, mapped to OpenADR 3.0 and IEEE 2030.5 event payloads, which carry price and event signals but not legal eligibility). RTOs, utilities and aggregators query it before calling an engine. Step three, once regulators accept the format, is clearing and settlement of permit-cleared MW across the registry.
mutants.why_now: Texas SB 6 (2025) makes disclosure and directed deployment of backup generation a legal duty for 75 MW+ loads, with an explicit emissions carve-out, so demand for exactly this record is forced by regulation. PJM is filing a reliability backstop and connect-and-manage framework, and Pennsylvania is pushing bring-your-own-generation rules. Turbines are sold out to about 2029-30. LLM extraction of permit conditions cuts the cost of structuring each site from consultant weeks to hours plus attorney QA. None of this existed at scale in 2019.
mutants.revenue_model: Onboarding and permit structuring of $15-40k per facility. SaaS of $3-6k per engine per year, which is about $25-50k a year for a 20 MW fleet of 8-10 engines. Aggregators and utilities pay a verification fee of roughly 0.5-1% of dispatch revenue that runs through certificates, and lenders, insurers and RTOs license the data ($100-300k a year). Illustrative scale: 5,000 engines is about $20M ARR, and the roughly 22,000 data center engines implied by 55 GW at 2.5 MW each is about $90M. Wider standby fleets would multiply that several times.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The scarce commodity is not megawatts or even permits. It is remaining permitted run-hours, a finite annual budget per engine, and nobody keeps that ledger neutrally. Whoever holds the ledger regulators trust becomes the rail everyone else must query, and the aggregators cannot build it because they profit from dispatch and cannot credibly police themselves. This inverts the parent: instead of pushing MW into the grid and hoping regulators follow, make regulators' comfort the product. Regulators have said no partly because they cannot see run hours. The registry supplies that visibility and could become the reason a permit is granted with conditions. It also creates network economies (every consumer of the certificate raises the value of being in it) and switching costs, since compliance history is an audit record.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: ship a software-only SB 6 and Title V ledger MVP (permit parsing plus hour-meter ingest plus report generation) and publish the Dispatch Eligibility Certificate v0.1 schema openly. Days 5-30: contact compliance leads at 20 Texas 75 MW+ operators and offer five pilots at $15k with a fixed-format SB 6 backup-generation disclosure pack. Days 10-30: hold informal briefings with TCEQ and VA DEQ staff to test whether an electronic ledger is acceptable as a compliance record, and get consumption LOIs (free API in exchange for feedback) from at least one aggregator. The riskiest assumption is regulator acceptance, so test it in the first month. Retain an air attorney to review the legal-basis tagging.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Voltus and CPower are dispatchers, and Voltus's Google deal covers batteries and thermostats, not generators or permits. They are conflicted as ledger-keepers and are natural certificate consumers, so we court them as design partners. ERock sells and operates its own gas hardware. OEM telemetry (Cat, Cummins and similar) is per-brand, not independent, and does not map runs to permit legal basis. DCIM and EHS software log air data but do not answer 'may I dispatch this engine now'. OpenADR and IEEE 2030.5 carry signals, not legality, so we build on them rather than compete. Trinity sells hourly permit projects, not a live neutral record, and could be a channel for onboarding. Note that the comparisons to OEM, DCIM and EHS vendors rest on my background knowledge, not verified this session.

mutants.title: Walkaway: PBM Offer Modeler Sold Through Associations
mutants.one_liner: A local-first tool that turns an independent pharmacy's own remits and invoices into a keep-or-drop answer for each January 1 PBM network offer, sold as a member benefit through state pharmacy associations.
mutants.customer: Wedge: owner-operators of 1-3 store independent pharmacies (roughly 40k-120k Rx a year) in one launch state, on PioneerRx, BestRx, Rx30 or QS/1, who have a 2027 network offer from at least one Big 3 PBM sitting on the desk. Buyer of record is the state pharmacy association (member-benefit license). Daily user is the owner-pharmacist plus their bookkeeper or accountant. Employers are not a customer at launch.
mutants.problem: Every Q4 an independent gets a take-it-or-leave-it PBM offer with about 30 days to answer, and the PBM implies that declining forfeits about a quarter of the business. The owner cannot answer two questions. First, what does this PBM's book actually earn per Rx after my real invoice cost and my cost to dispense? Second, what does walking away really cost in lost patients and front-store sales? The PSAO negotiates on the owner's behalf, but it is structurally conflicted (wholesaler-owned or fee-dependent; a hypothesis to verify in interviews). The alternative is an accountant with a spreadsheet at $150-250 an hour. Judges' and researcher's flaws this version fixes: the two-sided cold start (this version needs no employer and no pool to deliver value), the confidentiality and antitrust exposure (raw data never leaves the pharmacy), the missing evidence of willingness to pay (priced per decision, sold through a trusted channel), and a product that cannot be built from scratch before January (concierge first, parsers second).
mutants.solution: The pharmacy loads 12 months of 835 remits (or PDF remits, parsed on the machine by OCR and an LLM), its PMS dispensing export (Rx number, NDC, quantity, date) and wholesaler invoice lines. Everything runs in the browser or a local desktop app; nothing uploads. Output: (1) contribution margin per Rx by PBM, drug class and NDC, using true acquisition cost rather than NADAC alone, with underwater claims listed. (2) An offer model: enter the 2027 terms (MAC or NADAC-based schedule, dispensing fee, network fees, effective-rate true-ups) and the tool replays them on the last year's actual claims mix. (3) Walkaway math: patients on that PBM, refill-sync and front-store overlap, and retention scenarios (transfer, cash-pay, delivery) yield net annual profit if you sign versus decline. Sometimes the answer is that you make more money by dropping the book. (4) A one-page counter-ask with fee floors. (5) Opt-in give-to-get: contribute a k-anonymized summary (10+ contributing pharmacies per cell, 90-day lag, run by a third party under counsel's rules) to unlock peer percentiles. Guardrail: each pharmacy models and decides alone; the product never aggregates or signals intentions, which avoids group-boycott risk. The employer spread audit is a later output of the pool, not a launch product.
mutants.why_now: Today is late September and 2027 network offers are landing now, so there is a hard decision date. Closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens shutting about 1,200 stores) have made owners nervous and associations eager to show member value as membership shrinks. Browser-side OCR and LLM parsing of messy remits makes local-first onboarding a one-day job. A July 2026 open-source tool (rx-gap-finder, BestRx exports, runs client-side) shows owners will run this kind of analysis on their own machines, but it stops at spread by NDC. This would have been a consulting project in 2019.
mutants.revenue_model: Pharmacy: $299 per PBM offer analyzed, or a $749 season pass (all offers this cycle plus a mid-year re-check). Association: $8k-25k a year license for a member portal, co-branding and an aggregate state dashboard. Accountants and consultants serving pharmacies: white-label at about $1,500 per client. Illustrative bottom-up: 5 states x 300 paying pharmacies x $749 is about $1.1M, plus about $75k in association licenses. Ceiling on this product alone is about $13M (roughly 17-18k independents x $749), which is why the contributed pool is the platform for later index and employer-audit products.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The product being sold is not a benchmark, it is a priced exit. Owners usually already suspect the rates are bad; they sign because they cannot put a number on walking away, and the PBM's 25% threat fills the vacuum. A credible walkaway number changes the negotiation and works with a sample of one, so it solves the cold start that kills two-sided data businesses. Second, local-first architecture is what unlocks the association channel: associations will not hold members' claims (liability, antitrust), but they will happily license a tool that never touches the data.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls through one state association's executive director and board; ask directly whether the PSAO already offers contract modeling. Sign a letter of intent for a webinar and member email titled 'Model your 2027 offers.' Days 7-21: build 835 plus PDF-remit parsers for the three biggest PBM formats and PioneerRx and BestRx export mappers, and run the first 10 analyses by hand on screen share (free, in exchange for a case study and consent to use anonymized aggregates). Days 14-28: get a healthcare-antitrust attorney memo on data terms, the unilateral-decision guardrail and the aggregation thresholds. By day 30: 25 paid offer analyses ($299) and a $10k paid association pilot. Kill criterion: fewer than 8 of 20 owners say they would pay $299 to decide a live offer.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Truveris, Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx sell to employers from PBM-supplied claims and never touch pharmacy economics; this version sells to pharmacies and does not compete with employer audits at launch (they become the later buyers of the pool's output). rx-gap-finder is a single-PMS hobby project (0 stars) that flags underwater NDCs; it has no offer replay, no walkaway math, no peer percentiles and no distribution, so it is proof of demand and a free top-of-funnel rather than a rival. PQS/EQUIPP does adherence and quality for star ratings with no reimbursement modeling, and CPESN sells clinical services to payers; both are potential distribution partners, not product substitutes. 46brooklyn publishes public price research, not per-pharmacy decision tools. The unverified threat is PSAOs and PMS vendors; the wedge against them is neutrality (no wholesaler or PBM revenue) and, if a PSAO already offers modeling, the fallback is to white-label the engine to PSAOs.

mutants.title: Contingency Spread Recovery for Public Benefit Pools
mutants.one_liner: Zero-upfront PBM pass-through audits sold to school and local-government benefit pools, paid as a share of verified savings, using a shadow pharmacy price list built from local independents' remits, with a slice of each fee paid back to those pharmacies.
mutants.customer: Executive directors and boards of multi-employer public benefit pools: school-district benefit trusts and joint powers authorities, county-association and municipal-league health trusts, with 5,000-100,000 lives across dozens of member entities. They buy once for many districts, are subject to open-records and audit pressure, and carry political risk if a PBM overcharge surfaces. Secondary: single counties or districts of 300-3,000 lives (free pilot tier). Payer is the pool, only when savings are verified. No PBM ever pays us.
mutants.problem: A pool pays its PBM a billed price per NDC per claim, and its contract may promise pass-through, lowest-of pricing or audit rights. It cannot see what the PBM paid the pharmacy, so the audit rights only test billing against the PBM's own data. Consultants either charge flat fees on PBM-supplied files or are compensated in part by carriers and PBMs (disclosure of broker and consultant compensation is now required under the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act, though disclosure is not independence). Local officials also watch the town's last pharmacy close while the same PBM underpays it. The old obstacle was a claim-level join needing consent from both sides, which is why the parent's tie-out looked hard.
mutants.solution: (1) Shadow price list: 20-40 in-region independents contribute NDC-level paid unit price, fill date and BIN/PCN/group only (no patient identifiers), extracted locally. The team reconstructs, by week, what the PBM's retail network actually pays per NDC for the top 200-300 generics that drive most retail generic spend. (2) Tie-out to any plan: take the pool's own claims file (via contractual audit right or public-records request) and compare billed unit price per NDC and date to the reconstructed pharmacy-paid price, producing a spread per member per month by drug. The pharmacies never need to have filled that plan's claims, because a network's pharmacy MAC is common across clients. Scope is stated honestly as retail, and mail and specialty are excluded unless data exists. (3) Screen first: only take pools whose contracts promise pass-through or lowest-of pricing, or who will run an RFP; ordinary legal spread contracts yield renegotiation, not breach recovery. (4) Act: audit-rights letter, renegotiation, or an RFP among 3-5 bidders including the Big 3 and transparent PBMs. (5) Optional Local Access Rider: the pool redirects about 20% of verified savings into a per-Rx access fee paid to in-county independents, a plan-design choice that keeps pharmacies alive and makes them allies. Savings are verified by replaying 12 months post-change against the same shadow list, with a cap.
mutants.why_now: Local officials have political will after Rite Aid's exit and Walgreens' closures. Fiduciary and open-records pressure on PBM spend is rising, transparent PBMs give pools credible switch destinations, and federal and state reporting mandates create a paper trail to check (verify current scope). LLM and OCR parsing makes contributing remits a one-day task. January renewals also drive RFP timing, and pools' boards typically decide in Q4-Q1.
mutants.revenue_model: Contingency of 12-15% of first-year verified savings, with a floor for pools over 10,000 lives. Illustrative: a 20,000-life pool spends roughly $25-30M a year on drugs; a 4-8% price gap is $1-2M and a 12% share is $120-240k. Recurring Pass-Through Monitor after the audit at about $0.30-0.40 per member per month ($70-95k a year for 20,000 lives). Data co-op dividend: 15-20% of fees paid to contributing pharmacies pro rata as a fair-market-value data license (never tied to referrals; structure with counsel, and keep it away from any federal program business). A few hundred such pools nationally make this a $30M-100M revenue niche.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The employer does not need the claims the pharmacies saw. A PBM's retail pharmacy price list is common across clients in a network tier, so a crowd of pharmacies can reconstruct the hidden list once and any plan's billed prices can be compared to it. That turns a two-party consent-and-join problem into a price-list problem, and each additional pool costs almost nothing to audit. Contingency plus zero PBM money creates the only auditor with clean hands in a field where advisors are paid by the counterparties. Public bodies can compel data that private employers cannot, and the Local Access Rider turns the pharmacies from data suppliers into political allies.
mutants.first_30_days: Pick one state with many independents and public pools. Days 1-10: recruit 20 pharmacies through the state association, offering a free margin report in exchange for NDC-level price extracts; build the shadow list for the top 200 generics. Days 10-25: offer one county or district (300-3,000 lives) a free pilot, obtain its claims file by consent or open-records request, and produce a one-page spread letter with a dollars-per-member figure. Days 20-30: take the letter to a pool's executive director and broker and negotiate a contingency letter agreement (12% of verified savings, no fee if zero). Hire a healthcare attorney for data-license and dividend terms. Kill criterion: the pilot shows under 2% spread on retail generics, or fewer than 12 pharmacies agree to contribute.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Truveris and benefits consultants start from what the PBM hands over and charge fixed fees or carry PBM-linked compensation; this starts from the price the pharmacy was actually paid, is paid only on verified savings, and takes no PBM money. They are also possible channel partners for pools that already use them. Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx are the bidders and landing spots the audit sends pools toward, and we take no referral fee from them, which keeps the audit credible; they also cannot verify their own pass-through claims without a third party's pharmacy data. rx-gap-finder is a pharmacy-only underwater-Rx flagger with no employer price side. PQS and CPESN are recruiting channels for pharmacies, not competitors. The target is public pools and counties, a segment the competitor research did not show any of them serving, but this is unverified and should be checked in interviews.

mutants.title: The Pharmacy-Verified Reimbursement Index
mutants.one_liner: A furnisher-funded bureau, like a credit bureau for PBM payments, that turns what pharmacies actually pay and are actually paid into a reference index that state laws, Medicaid rate-setting and transparent-PBM contracts can cite, launching with a per-state Underwater Index sold to pharmacy associations for the 2027 legislative sessions.
mutants.customer: First six months: state pharmacy associations and their legal and lobbying arms in 3-5 states with active 2027 PBM agendas, at $25-60k per state per year. Next: state Medicaid pharmacy programs and state employee plans rebasing dispensing fees and ingredient-cost basis, departments of insurance enforcing below-cost and pay-parity laws, and TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs that want an external yardstick. Eventually: contracts that reference the index directly. Contributing pharmacies pay nothing and get a dividend.
mutants.problem: Everyone who needs a reference price for pharmacy reimbursement relies on an interested party or a slow survey. NADAC is a voluntary survey of acquisition costs that says nothing about dispensing cost or what any PBM actually paid. State cost-of-dispensing studies are periodic, commissioned from consultants, and stale by publication (typically low-to-mid six figures each; verify). Legislators cannot say how many claims are paid below cost or by whom, so reimbursement-floor and pay-parity laws are enforced only by complaint. PBMs face no neutral definition of a fair payment. The parent's insight (pharmacies hold the ground-truth ledger) is stronger as infrastructure than as a one-off audit.
mutants.solution: Pharmacies use the free local-first margin report (same ingestion as a per-pharmacy tool) and opt in to contribute monthly aggregates: paid price and invoice cost per NDC per PBM network per state, plus optionally allocated cost-to-dispense. The bureau publishes: (a) a State Underwater Index (share of claims paid below acquisition cost, by PBM, only where 10+ pharmacies and 5+ per PBM cell contribute, with a 90-day lag); (b) an invoice-based acquisition cost index by NDC-week; (c) a quarterly cost-of-dispensing panel; (d) a regulator API to test whether a network paid below the index in a given month. Design floor for antitrust: a third-party-run exchange following the withdrawn 1996 health-care information-exchange conditions (5+ contributors, no contributor over 25% weight, data 3+ months old), plus counsel sign-off. Credibility: published methodology, an independent standards board (pharmacist, health economist, antitrust counsel, ex-regulator) and a sample audit by an accounting firm. Flywheel: an association buys the evidence pack, a law cites the index, the regulator needs the feed, contracts reference the index, and more pharmacies contribute for the dividend (25% of index revenue, pro rata by verified contribution).
mutants.why_now: A wave of state PBM reimbursement and transparency laws has arrived just as closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores, Drug Channels' August 2026 'K-shaped shakeout') give legislators a reason to demand numbers; 2027 sessions open in January and associations need evidence in Q4. The cost stack has collapsed: surveying a few hundred pharmacies by questionnaire costs six figures, but reading remits and invoices they already hold costs cents per claim now that OCR and LLM parsing handle messy formats and local-first processing removes the custody objection. This is a 2026 unlock, not a 2019 one.
mutants.revenue_model: Association evidence pack plus monthly index: $25-60k per state per year (target 3 states by month 6, about $100-150k). State Medicaid and employee-plan data licenses: $100-400k per state per year after a track record. DOI compliance feed: $50-150k. API licenses for TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs: $25-100k. Index-in-contract licensing: about $0.02-0.05 per member per month, comparable to index-licensing models in other markets. Pharmacies: free plus a 25% revenue dividend. A 30-state footprint could plausibly support $10-30M a year.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Standards win by being cited in statutes and contracts, and NADAC became the reference by being neutral, not by being complete. A pharmacy-verified index earns legitimacy differently, because it comes from invoices and remits (facts, not survey opinion), and it is the only source that can measure paid versus cost per PBM, which is exactly what a below-cost reimbursement law needs in order to be enforced. Associations fund the first index as lobbying evidence, the resulting laws then create a compliance buyer (the regulator), and each citation adds switching cost. The more PBM-owned pharmacies dominate the market, the more the independents' ledger is the only independent counterfactual.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 2 states with an active 2027 PBM agenda and pitch the association executive directors: 'your state's Underwater Report by December 15 for session prep, co-branded.' Days 5-25: recruit 25 contributing pharmacies per state with a free margin report; run 6 months of remits and invoices through a local script by hand (concierge). Days 10-20: retain antitrust counsel for a 10-page methodology and thresholds memo, and seat a 5-person advisory board. Day 20-30: ask a state DOI or Medicaid pharmacy director for a 30-minute meeting on what they would need to enforce existing rules. By day 30: 2 signed letters of intent at about $25k and 40 contributing pharmacies. By day 60: first anonymized state index published. Kill criterion: no association will pay $25k for a state report before the session opens.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Truveris and other employer-audit firms analyze PBM-supplied claims for individual clients; this sells neutral reference data to governments, associations and payers, and those firms can be licensees. Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx market transparency but cannot certify it themselves, so the index is a potential licensed yardstick for them. rx-gap-finder is a one-pharmacy tool with no pool, no network effect and no legitimacy with regulators. PQS/EQUIPP holds 65,000 connected pharmacies but sells adherence and quality to plans, and adding payer-adverse reimbursement data would strain those relationships (hypothesis, unverified). CPESN's 3,500 pharmacies are a contribution channel. 46brooklyn's public research is a natural academic advisor or co-publisher, not a substitute, because it cannot see paid amounts. Gap in the parent's competitor scan: state cost-of-dispensing survey vendors and the CMS NADAC contractor were not researched, so verify whether they are building continuous invoice-based products before committing.

mutants.title: Stack-Pooled 24/7 Article 14 Desk for Non-EU Brands
mutants.one_liner: A guaranteed-SLA Assigned Representative that files CRA Article 14 reports for 50-250 person non-EU connected-device brands, doing the triage once per shared component stack (Tuya, ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek) and fanning it out to every client on that stack.
mutants.customer: Medium-sized (50-250 staff, above the small-enterprise fine exemption) non-EU smart-home, e-mobility and networking brands based in Shenzhen, Taiwan, Korea and the US that sell into the EU via Amazon EU and retail. Their firmware comes from an ODM on one of 3 shared stacks: Tuya/Matter modules, ESP-IDF/ESP32, or OpenWrt/Realtek SDKs. The buyer is the head of product or compliance; the introduction comes through the EU Responsible Person/EPR (WEEE and packaging) service providers who already serve these sellers.
mutants.problem: These brands do not know what is inside their own firmware because the ODM built it, so they cannot tell whether a KEV/EUVD entry hits them. They have no one awake in Europe at 3am Sunday to decide 'actively exploited, affects us, file'. The 72h and 14-day clocks carry fines even if the 24h clock does not, and their EU retail partners will start asking for proof of process. Existing options each miss part of this. Software (CVD Portal, CRACI, Regulus) stops at timers and drafts, with filing left to the customer. Finite State and H-X draft notices but leave filing to the customer. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 or price. EcoComply is an AR mandate with no triage.
mutants.solution: Three things in one contract. (1) Named-analyst AR mandate plus a written SLA: triage decision within 4h and early warning filed inside 24h, weekends included, under a client-approved decision tree and pre-authorised actions. (2) Stack-pooled triage: a stack owner analyses each exploited entry once against the stack's component graph and issues per-firmware-version pre-approved VEX and notice drafts to every enrolled brand on that stack, so a client-named analyst only checks the version delta and files. (3) Firmware-fingerprint onboarding: the brand uploads a firmware image or OTA URL and the desk builds the component list itself, removing the missing-SBOM problem. Every KEV/EUVD entry also gets a timestamped per-product 'affected / not affected' decision, delivered monthly as a signed monitoring evidence log. That log is the recurring deliverable when nothing was exploited, and it is what retailers and market surveillance authorities will ask for. The 24h and 72h drills run on the client's own stack.
mutants.why_now: Article 14 reporting went live on 11 Sep 2026 (about 18 days ago) and the ENISA SRP opened the same day. Patchstack shows managed filing is now legal and being productised, so the window before it becomes a checkbox is roughly 6-12 months. Retail supplier manuals are being rewritten for the Dec 2027 full application, and GPSR (since Dec 2024) already trained these sellers to buy EU-representative services.
mutants.revenue_model: Base fee of about EUR 3.6-4.8k per year per product family (AR mandate, stack monitoring, monthly evidence log, one drill), well above EcoComply's EUR 1.5k AR-only anchor but below a monthly PSIRT retainer. Filing events cost EUR 1.5-3k each. Tabletop drills and 'clock audit' are EUR 1.5-5k. Wholesale white-label 24/7 back-end capacity is sold to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and SBOM platforms. Target is 100 product families by month 12 (about EUR 400k ARR). One stack analyst covering 30-100 clients keeps gross margin above 65%.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not filing, it is the stack-to-firmware truth table. Brands do not know what is inside, but the desk sees which SDK forks and versions actually ship across dozens of brands. That is a cornered resource that a one-off consultancy cannot copy: each new client on a stack has near-zero marginal analyst cost and improves the fingerprint coverage. Also, 95% of what the desk produces is 'not affected'. Selling signed negative evidence as the monthly deliverable fixes the judges' 'insurance nobody buys until audited' flaw. Targeting 50-250 person firms sidesteps the Art 64(10) small-enterprise exemption on the 24h fine.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: get a professional-indemnity quote, and get written confirmation from ENISA or a national CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts. Get counsel to settle how the 24h clock starts when the desk detects first, and draft the AR mandate and decision tree. Weeks 1-2: build component graphs for 3 stacks (ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek, Tuya) covering the top 25 exploited component families of the last 24 months, using open-source firmware unpacking such as EMBA. Weeks 2-4: sell a EUR 1.5k '24h drill + firmware fingerprint' to 20 brands sourced from 3 EPR/GPSR representative providers and Amazon-EU seller communities. The drill simulates an exploited entry hitting their stack and measures their real time-to-decision. Convert 5 into annual AR+desk contracts. Contract 3 part-time named analysts across time zones and confirm the SRP login rules apply to them.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: It refuses the generic 'PSIRT retainer' frame owned by TridentSec, Finite State and Cybellum. It sells the one thing they call customer-owned, which is a contractually guaranteed filing as the named AR. It uses the SBOM and monitoring layer (CVD Portal at EUR 99/mo, CRACI, Zealience, ONEKEY) as commodity input rather than product. It is aimed at non-EU mid-size brands, which Cybellum's enterprise focus and Patchstack's free open-source-only service do not serve. Its economics come from pooling by stack, which per-client consultancies and per-seat platforms cannot match. Incumbent MSSPs and certification bodies (Kudelski, TUV SUD, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas) become white-label distributors rather than rivals, since the desk offers them the back end they lack.

mutants.title: Retailer-Mandated Vulnerability Desk, Paid by Suppliers
mutants.one_liner: EU retailers and distributors put the desk on their approved-provider list for connected private-label and marketplace products, and their non-EU suppliers pay per SKU family, the way suppliers already pay retailer-nominated test labs, while the retailer gets a live exposure dashboard for its whole connected catalogue.
mutants.customer: Mandating party: product-compliance heads at mid-size EU consumer-electronics, DIY, sports (e-bikes), toy and discount retailers and distributors with 50-2,000 connected SKUs, including own-brand ranges. Payers: the 20-200 non-EU suppliers and ODMs behind those SKUs, each paying for the product families it sells to that retailer.
mutants.problem: A retailer that sells connected products under its own name is treated as the CRA manufacturer (to confirm with counsel), and an importer or distributor must chase unreachable non-EU suppliers when a vulnerability appears. Retailers have no view of which of their 1,800 connected SKUs contain the component in this morning's exploited-vulnerability headline. Their suppliers will not share firmware willingly and cannot show a 24h capability. The parent's problem is that small makers will not buy a desk they see as insurance. Here the party with the pain is not the party with the budget, and the retailer holds the leverage over the supplier.
mutants.solution: Product 1 is a retailer-paid 'Connected Range Exposure Baseline'. The desk collects firmware for 25-50 SKUs, which the retailer can compel from suppliers. It unpacks them, builds the component lists, checks current exposure to KEV/EUVD, tests each supplier's vulnerability-contact deliverability, and delivers a supplier-requirement clause for the next supplier manual. Product 2 is the ongoing service. The retailer's supplier manual names the desk (and any equivalent that passes its audit) as an approved provider. Each supplier enrols product families and the desk becomes its AR and 24/7 filing service, with stack-pooled triage. The retailer sees a live dashboard: for each SKU, affected, not affected or unknown, with supplier response time, supporting delist or recall decisions and its own regulatory file. The desk's fan-out model is reused, but the sales motion is one retailer mandate that brings in many suppliers.
mutants.why_now: CRA reporting has been live since 11 Sep 2026 and retailer supplier manuals are being rewritten ahead of Dec 2027. RED delegated-act cybersecurity rules (in force since Aug 2025) and GPSR (since Dec 2024) have already taught retail compliance teams to demand supplier documents and chase non-EU suppliers, so the workflow and budget owner exist. Retail groups have not yet named a vulnerability-reporting provider, so early mandates set the approved list.
mutants.revenue_model: Retailer-paid baseline of EUR 10-25k per range as the first sale. Dashboard licence of EUR 15-40k/yr per retailer. Supplier-paid subscription of EUR 600-1,200 per product family per year (falling with volume), plus EUR 1.5-3k per filing event, contractually paid by the supplier. One mid-size retailer with about 150 connected SKU families across 60 suppliers yields roughly EUR 100-130k/yr. Ten retailers gives roughly EUR 1M+ ARR with sales cost amortised across 60 or more payers per mandate.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Change the buyer chain, not the product. Retail supply chains already run on the 'nominated lab' pattern, where the buyer mandates a provider and the supplier pays, and testing spend per product (EN 18031 or similar) dwarfs a EUR 600-1,200 annual desk fee, so suppliers barely resist. The dashboard turns a rare-event insurance product into something a compliance head opens every morning. And retail is the only place where a 24/7 filer has real leverage, because the retailer can delist a supplier that does not respond.
mutants.first_30_days: Identify 15 EU retail and distribution product-compliance heads via GPSR, RED and product-safety forums and trade-association events. Pitch each a EUR 12k baseline on 25-50 own-brand SKUs, with the deliverable being an exposure table plus supplier scorecard plus draft supplier-manual clause. Publish the clause as a free template through retail associations to seed demand. Sign 2 paying baselines by day 30-45. Use the baselines to build the first supplier cohorts (20-40 suppliers) and open partnership talks with SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas and TUV, who hold the current nominated-lab relationships, about white-labelling the 24/7 back end.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: None of the competitors in the parent's research sells to retailers. Finite State, Cybellum, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, EcoComply, H-X and the SBOM vendors all sell to manufacturers one at a time, paying a high customer-acquisition cost per maker, and Patchstack is free and open-source only. One retailer mandate replaces dozens of separate maker sales. The obvious threat is certification bodies and labs, which sell one-off per-model reports while a 24/7 desk has the opposite cost structure, so they are better treated as distribution partners. Switching costs come from integration with the retailer's PLM and supplier-onboarding flow, and from the supplier cohort already enrolled, which a copycat would have to win over from scratch.

mutants.title: Outside-In Product Security Ratings for Insurers and Buyers
mutants.one_liner: Invert the desk: instead of helping one maker meet the 24-hour clock, independently measure from the outside whether thousands of connected-product makers can, and how exposed their shipped firmware is, and sell the scores and accumulation data to insurers, fleet buyers and lenders.
mutants.customer: First buyers: cyber and product-liability insurers and MGAs writing hardware and IoT makers, who need product-level exposure and accumulation data. Second: B2B fleet and infrastructure buyers (EV-charging operators, micromobility fleets, smart-building integrators, telcos buying CPE) that run supplier due diligence. Third: lenders and PE firms doing diligence on hardware brands. Manufacturers do not buy scores. They pay only for evidence review and remediation (a funnel to the desk).
mutants.problem: Every maker will soon say 'we comply' with the CRA, but the declarations are self-assessed and unverified until a market surveillance authority acts, which is slow and under-resourced. Insurers have no product-level model of accumulation, even though one exploited component hits every device on that stack. That is a catastrophe-modelling problem with no model. Procurement teams rely on questionnaires. The 24-hour clock is uniquely measurable: it is a dated, binary behaviour, unlike vague 'security posture', but nobody measures it from outside.
mutants.solution: A rating built outside-in from three layers. (a) Clock-readiness signals: security.txt, a published CVD policy, a working vulnerability contact, advisory history, stated support period, update cadence, and time-to-acknowledge on a clearly labelled contact-verification probe. (b) Firmware exposure: public firmware and OTA images, plus purchased units for top SKUs, unpacked and matched against exploited-vulnerability feeds to give a component list, exposure count and stack cluster. (c) Portfolio accumulation: for an insurer's book of insureds or a fleet buyer's supplier list, how many share a stack with a newly exploited component (the correlation number). Makers get a right of reply and can submit evidence, but cannot pay to change a score. Method: month 0-3 process-signal ratings for about 500 brands across e-mobility, smart home, routers, chargers, cameras and wearables; month 3-6 firmware exposure on the top 200 SKUs and the first accumulation reports. A separate analyst team runs the desk as the remediation upsell, behind a conflict-of-interest firewall.
mutants.why_now: The reporting duty went live on 11 Sep 2026, so 'time to report' just became a legal, checkable behaviour. Insurers are pricing CRA-driven product liability for the first time. Outside-in ratings are a proven category for company networks, and firmware unpacking is now cheap through open-source tooling and LLM-assisted triage. No dominant product-level rating exists.
mutants.revenue_model: Data licences of EUR 25-80k/yr per insurer or MGA; EUR 6-15k/yr per fleet operator or integrator per category; EUR 3-8k per diligence report for lenders and PE; EUR 2-5k per maker for evidence review; desk upsell as a funnel. Long term the rating is written into insurance pricing and procurement clauses ('supplier must hold a score of B or better'), giving standard-setter economics with a data moat.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Insurers care about accumulation more than any single score, and the desk's pooled stack graph is exactly an accumulation model, so the same data serves the desk and the rating. Real filings and drills, with consent and anonymised, give a calibration set showing which outside-in signals predict actual time-to-report, and that validation is what makes a rating credible. Every desk client both funds and calibrates the rating. Flaw of the inversion: legal risk (defamation, unauthorised access), which is why probes are labelled, analysis uses lawfully obtained units and public images, scores are aggregated and methodology is public.
mutants.first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: build a crawler over 500 brands in 6 categories to score security.txt, CVD page, contact deliverability, advisory history and support-period statements. Week 2: send a benign, clearly labelled contact-verification probe and record response times. Week 3: publish a free report, 'State of vulnerability-reporting readiness among 500 connected-product brands' (for example, what share have no working vulnerability contact weeks after the duty began), to earn press and insurer attention. Weeks 3-4: hold 20 discovery calls with cyber/product-liability underwriters, MGAs and fleet operators, and offer paid pilots of EUR 8-15k to score their insureds or suppliers. Aim for one signed pilot by day 45 and confirm that no insurer-grade product rating already exists before scaling.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: The parent's competitors (Finite State, Cybellum, ONEKEY, Cybeats, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, CRACI) all work inside-out for the manufacturer's own firmware or workflow and are paid by the maker. This business is outside-in and paid by the party that bears the risk, so none of them competes for that buyer, and several become data suppliers. From general knowledge, not verified in this session: company-level ratings such as BitSight and SecurityScorecard score networks, not shipped products; certification schemes (ioXt, ETSI EN 303 645-based tests, UL programmes) are pass/fail, point-in-time and manufacturer-paid; consumer-testing NGOs publish periodic tests. Large MSSPs and certification bodies are conflicted because manufacturers pay them. The moat is the calibrated stack graph, the methodology and eventual adoption in insurance and procurement contracts.

mutants.title: Section-Level Hydrogen and Helium Leads for Landmen
mutants.one_liner: Sell 90-day exclusive, page-linked lists of Nemaha-corridor sections with hydrogen or helium evidence buried in old mud logs, DST reports and driller notes, to the landmen and lease shops who spend the first dollars of every junior's program.
mutants.customer: Independent landmen and lease-brokerage shops (2-50 people) in Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma who assemble acreage for natural hydrogen and helium juniors, plus the roughly 40-120 junior explorers themselves (Rystad counts 40, AKAP counts 123 companies). Wedge buyer: the lease shop, because it is paid per acre leased, has a hard deadline (leases are taken in a rush after each well announcement), and has no geoscientist on staff.
mutants.problem: The free datasets (USGS/BLM 16,000 gas analyses, KGS OFR 2025-59, SMU/GDR temperatures) already give away the structured layers, so an atlas built on them is worthless. What they omit is the unstructured evidence in page images at KCC/KGS-type archives: mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test gas notes, driller remarks such as 'gas would not burn', 'non-flammable' or 'heavy N2 odor', and water-well gas notes. Landmen today pick where to lease by copying the footprint of the last press release, which means they arrive after the price of a lease has already moved. Juniors that do this in-house (HyTerra, MAX Power, Koloma) are not customers, so the sellable market is the long tail and the lease shops serving it.
mutants.solution: A curated evidence-card product for one live fairway (Nemaha Uplift and Midcontinent Rift, KS/NE/OK). A VLM pipeline reads page images for a defined set of document types, a geologist verifies every card that reaches a customer, and each card carries the page image, the quoted text, and a confidence grade for sampling method, air-contamination signs (N2/O2 ratio) and analytical era. Cards roll up to a ranked list of 30-60 sections per block, plus a short 'do not lease' list of sections with clean hydrocarbon gas and no signal, which saves buyers money. Free layers (USGS, KGS, BLM/state mineral ownership) are ingested as baseline and shown for context but never sold. Delivered as a GeoPackage/KMZ and a PDF, with a courtroom-simple audit trail so a landman can defend the pick to a junior's board. Geothermal is dropped from v1 because SMU/GDR and GeoMap give it away.
mutants.why_now: Natural hydrogen went from about 10 to 40+ searching companies since 2020 (Rystad) and 123 by AKAP's count; HyTerra's Kansas McCoy 1 result (up to 83-96% H2) turned the Nemaha corridor into an active lease play in 2025-26, so lease shops need defensible picks right now. VLMs now read typed and handwritten well forms at cents per page, which broke the cost barrier that made a section-level re-read uneconomic before 2024. State surveys (KGS/KCC) are releasing more scans, and the academic OCR/LLM methods are public, which lowers the technical risk for a two-person team while making curation and speed the real product.
mutants.revenue_model: Entry pack: $5k non-exclusive, 3-township block. Exclusive block: $12-20k for a 90-day first-look on a 6-10 township block, renewable. Success fee: a capped per-net-acre finder fee (for example $2-5) or 0.5% ORRI on leases taken from exclusive-block sections. Year-1 bottom-up: 25 entry packs ($125k) + 6 exclusive blocks ($90k) + fees (~$50k) is about $265k with a two-person team; the business scales by adding fairways (Michigan/Ohio Rift extension, Colorado, Texas Panhandle helium) rather than by raising price per corridor. The buyer's ROI check: a 20,000-acre lease program at even $20-50/acre bonus is $0.4-1M, so a $5-15k pack is single-digit percent of spend.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The product is not data, it is time-boxed scarcity. Lease information is perishable: once one buyer signs, the price of that section moves, so the value of a lead decays over weeks, and the right pricing unit is a 90-day exclusive option on a block, exactly how prospect generators sell in oil and gas. Second, the 0.5% hit rate seen in the Paris Basin OCR study (26 wells of about 5,000) is a weakness for a broad atlas but a strength for a precision shortlist: sell 40 sections, not 40,000, and let the 'do not lease' list carry the rest of the value. Third, buyers who drill a lead and share the result get a discount, and those results become a private ground-truth set that calibrates the confidence score, which no free dataset can copy.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: pick the Nemaha corridor counties in Kansas, download KGS/KCC scanned ACO-1 forms, driller logs, DST reports and mud logs for about 5,000 wells, and run VLM extraction on the four document types. Week 2: have a geologist verify the top 150 candidate cards and produce a 60-section block map with page-image links. Week 3: contact 10 lease shops and 10 juniors (LinkedIn plus the AAPL and Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association member lists) with one free sample card and a demo map. Week 4: ask for a $5k prepay for the block pack. Kill test from the parent: if fewer than 3 of 10 prepay, stop and go to the state-survey channel instead. Also offer an exclusive 90-day option on the sections buyers like best.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: USGS/BLM, KGS, SMU/GDR, GeoMap and EPRI: we sell only what they omit (unstructured page-level evidence and curated section lists) and use them free as baseline, so a free download cannot replace the product. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar: they hold their own in-house archives and are not customers, and our buyers are the lease shops and the long tail they cannot serve. NthDS and Enverus/TGS: they sell per-well files ($70-80 LAS) to O&G buyers and have no hydrogen or helium curation; they are more likely acquirer or data partner than rival, and our per-section conclusion with a human-verified audit trail is a different unit. Heologic, AKAP, Wood Mackenzie, Rystad: they sell company- or project-level intelligence or soil-gas anomalies, not lease-block, page-linked evidence. Terra AI and HyReveal model, but lack the extracted page-level inputs. Geothermal (Zanskar, GeoMap, SMU/GDR) is deliberately excluded.

mutants.title: Plug-or-Pitch: Turning Idle Wells Into Assets
mutants.one_liner: Screen idle and orphan oil wells for hydrogen, helium and heat evidence, and get paid a share of the plugging liability that disappears when a well is transferred to an explorer who wants a ready-made hole to the basement.
mutants.customer: The payer is the liability holder, not the explorer. Wedge: independent operators in Kansas and Oklahoma holding 50-500 idle, shut-in or temporarily abandoned wells under rising plugging and bonding pressure. Phase 2: state orphan-well programs (funded by the $4.7B IIJA orphan-well money) and state land offices. The other side of the transaction, who takes the well and pays a placement fee, is a hydrogen, helium or geothermal junior that today drills new holes at seven-figure cost.
mutants.problem: An idle well is a negative asset: plugging often costs tens of thousands of dollars per well (an estimate to confirm state by state), and operators or states carry that liability for years. Meanwhile the parent idea's buyers spend roughly seven figures to drill a test hole to basement, and a wellbore that already penetrates basement, with a file that shows non-flammable gas or elevated temperature, is worth many multiples of its plugging cost to them. The two sides never find each other because the evidence sits in scanned well files, and juniors in the parent's research 'do not budget $15-50k a year for data' but do budget hard money for holes. Price anchored to a known plugging cost is a much easier sale than price anchored to speculative exploration value.
mutants.solution: A per-well 'Reuse Dossier' built from each idle well's own file and its offsets: hydrogen/helium/N2-rich gas shows from mud logs, DSTs and driller notes, depth to basement, casing/cement/plugging status, bottom-hole temperature and gradient, and produced-water chemistry, each with page-image provenance and a confidence grade. A Reuse Score estimates re-entry cost against new-drill cost and states the single test that would confirm the lead. Wells are bundled into small re-entry lots and placed with repurposers under a recorded assignment of plugging liability (with state transfer approval and financial assurance), often keeping a retained royalty or carry for the seller. The operator pays nothing upfront: screening is free and the startup is paid from the avoided liability and from the placement. Geothermal scoring can be sourced from partners such as WellScout AI rather than built.
mutants.why_now: State and federal pressure on idle wells is at its peak: IIJA orphan-well plugging money is flowing through the late 2020s, and states have built lists that did not exist five years ago. Hydrogen and helium juniors raised $20M-$245M rounds (Koloma, Terra AI, Mantle8) and HyTerra proved that twinning historic wells works, so demand for cheap access to basement-penetrating holes is real. VLM extraction cost per well file has collapsed to a few dollars, which makes free screening for an operator affordable on a contingency basis; that would have been uneconomic in 2022.
mutants.revenue_model: Contingent success fee of about 15% of the avoided plugging cost (from the operator or state) when a well transfers, plus a $10-25k placement fee (or 5% of any bonus or sale price) from the repurposer, plus $500-1,500 for a premium dossier and a $10-25k/year 'reuse lot' feed for juniors. Illustrative unit economics: an operator with 200 idle wells costs about $16k to screen (about $80/well compute plus geologist review); if 1-2% clear the bar (1-2 wells above the 0.5% Paris Basin rate is plausible for a targeted fairway) and each saves about $40k of plugging cost, revenue is $6-12k in liability fees plus placement fees per portfolio, and a state program is 10-50x that. The wedge is deliberately contingent so the customer has no downside.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The bid-ask spread has the wrong sign: the holder sees a negative asset (minus the plugging cost) and the explorer sees a hole worth a multiple of its plugging cost, and the only missing ingredient is verified evidence about which wells sit on the positive side. Low hit rate (about 0.5% in the Paris Basin study) kills a subscription atlas but not a contingency screen, because the operator's cost is zero and one hit pays for the portfolio. The startup's true asset is not the data but the transferable, state-approved playbook for liability assignment plus a book of buyers, which creates a two-sided market that data vendors and free datasets cannot replicate.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: pull the public inactive/TA well lists from the Kansas KCC and Oklahoma OCC and pick 300 wells that reach basement in the Nemaha corridor. Week 2: extract their files and offsets and produce 30 Reuse Dossiers with a scored top 10. Week 3: call 25 independent operators and the plugging-fund manager at one state agency with the offer 'give us your 100 worst idle wells, screening is free, we take 15% of the avoided plugging cost if we place a well'. In parallel get 2-3 juniors to sign non-binding LOIs to consider re-entry lots. Week 4: sign 3 contingency agreements and confirm with the state regulator what transfer-with-assumption of liability requires. Before building further, run 15 calls to check the two unverified assumptions: state transfer rules and re-entry cost versus a new drill.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: USGS/BLM, KGS, SMU/GDR and GeoMap: free datasets give regional or aggregate layers, none identifies which specific idle well is a transferable reuse candidate, so they are our inputs, not substitutes. WellScout AI is the closest overlap (screens oil wells for geothermal conversion); it covers only heat and sells software to operators, so we can partner on thermal scoring and win on multi-commodity gas evidence plus the transaction. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar keep their data in-house and are demand-side buyers of re-entry lots, not rivals. NthDS and Enverus/TGS sell files to buyers of O&G data; they do not take contingent fees on liability transfers and have channel conflict doing so. AKAP, Wood Mackenzie and Rystad sell market intelligence, not well-level transactions. Not covered in the parent's research and to be verified: oil-and-gas A&D brokers and state orphan-well reuse pilots.

mutants.title: Pumper-Sampled Hydrogen and Helium Ground-Truth Registry
mutants.one_liner: Stop digging through what the industry failed to measure and start measuring it: pay lease pumpers to grab wellhead gas samples, assay them for hydrogen and helium, and build the depth-tagged registry that becomes the standard for what is under the ground.
mutants.customer: Wedge: hydrogen, helium and geothermal explorers and their modelers (Koloma-type juniors outside their own acreage, HyTerra/MAX Power-type juniors, Terra AI, HyReveal) who commission sampling campaigns across a fairway. Contributors: small independent operators and the pumpers (lease operators) who visit each well weekly, starting with the Kansas and Oklahoma independents. Later payers: lenders, insurers and resource certifiers who need a standard, auditable measurement before they finance a discovery.
mutants.problem: Old well files are noisy for a structural reason: the industry never measured hydrogen or helium. Standard mud-logging and production gas analysis use flame-ionization detectors that cannot see H2 or He, so a 1935 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' note is an accident, contamination and sampling method are unknown, and the parent's archive is capped at about 16,000 free analyses and a 0.5% hit rate. Explorers who need to know where hydrogen and helium are today either drill blind, run private one-off campaigns, or use soil-gas anomalies. Nobody keeps a standardized, depth-tagged, contamination-corrected, fresh measurement for the roughly one million producing US wells or the tens of thousands of new holes drilled each year.
mutants.solution: A three-layer business. Layer 1 (first product, sellable in 6 months): buyer-commissioned sampling campaigns. A buyer specifies a transect or 200-well fairway; operators allow their pumpers to fill a $12 sample container at the casinghead or separator vent following a safety protocol; a bounty of about $25 goes to the pumper; samples go to a partner lab or an in-house GC-TCD unit, and the buyer gets H2/He/N2/CO2/Ar/O2/C1-C6 with GPS, photo, chain of custody and an air-contamination correction. Layer 2: a registry with an open measurement spec (sampling method, contamination QC, lab certification) and a contribution scheme: operators get a free full gas assay (which many already pay $50-150 for to support BTU, sales or flaring reports, a hypothesis to test), exclusive rights to their own well results for 90-180 days, and a revenue share. Layer 3: a certified add-on H2/He TCD channel for mud-logging contractors and geothermal drillers so every new hole feeds the registry, and a scoring layer that uses fresh samples to calibrate the archive-based confidence grades from the parent idea.
mutants.why_now: Hydrogen and helium explorers are funded (Koloma about $245M, Mantle8 EUR31M, Terra AI $20M with BHP and Khosla, 123 companies per AKAP) but starved of trustworthy labels, and the modelers (Terra AI, HyReveal) explicitly need fresh ground-truth data. Portable micro-GC/TCD analyzers and smartphone chain-of-custody have made distributed sampling cheap, and VLM tools make the old archive a cheap starting prior rather than the product. Geothermal and helium buyers want auditable data for financing, and no standard exists yet, which is the moment a standard can be set.
mutants.revenue_model: Sampling campaigns at about $250 per well (cost roughly $60-120 with in-house GC and $130-170 with outside labs); a 200-well campaign is about $50k. Registry subscriptions of $10-50k per basin per year for explorers and modelers. Data licenses to modelers and financiers. Lab certification and channel fees from mud-logging contractors. Optional later: small overriding royalties on leases taken over registry-flagged sections. Year-1 target: 1,500-3,000 wells sampled, 5-8 campaign customers (about $300-400k), 10 registry subscribers.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The right inversion is that data quality, not data availability, is the bottleneck: every archive layer the parent proposed is limited by a measurement nobody made. Because operators pay for gas analysis anyway, the marginal cost of adding H2 and He to a routine sample is almost zero, so the contributor network can be built with a bounty rather than a salesforce. The registry's moat is network economics plus a standard: contributors are also the sources, the modelers need the labels, and lenders will trust the one dataset with certified provenance. Fresh samples also calibrate the archive-derived confidence scores, so the parent idea becomes a cheap prior on top of a proprietary ground-truth set.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: contract a commercial gas lab that runs GC-TCD (or buy a used micro-GC with TCD for about $15-25k) and design the sample kit and safety protocol with an experienced pumper. Week 2: sign 2 independent operators (about 100 wells each, via the Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association and personal referrals) on the free-assay, 90-day-exclusive deal. Week 3: sample 100 wells across a transect crossing the Nemaha uplift and publish a one-page ground-truth map. Week 4: pitch 15 juniors and modelers a 200-well campaign at $250 per well with half prepaid, and ask HyReveal and Terra AI for a data-partner letter. Kill test: if no buyer prepays by week 6, sell the same samples as a section-level pack to landmen (see the sharpened offspring).
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: USGS/BLM (about 16,000 historical analyses, 2021) and KGS OFR 2025-59: static, mixed-quality historical compilations; our data is new, standardized and continuously growing, with QC they lack. SMU/GDR and GeoMap: temperature-focused and free; we sell direct gas chemistry. Heologic (helium-anomaly database and consulting): relies on subsoil helium proxies and sells services; we measure at-depth well gas at scale through a contributor network and an open spec. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar: proprietary data only in their own footprints; they become campaign buyers outside their acreage. Terra AI and HyReveal: modelers who lack labels, so they are customers and channel partners rather than competitors. NthDS and Enverus/TGS: software and data resellers with no field measurement network and no reason to build one, likely acquirers. Zanskar and WellScout AI: focused on geothermal; not a gas registry.

mutants.title: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense
mutants.one_liner: A $395, 48-hour kit for defense counsel that turns a letter-of-protection bill into line-by-line cross-examination questions and a signed rebuttal, with the testifying coder as the real profit center.
mutants.customer: Wedge: 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques in Houston-area and Atlanta-metro courts that take carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k. On those files a $3-5k billing expert usually needs carrier pre-approval or gets skipped. Buyer is the associate or partner running the file. Florida is a second-phase rebuttal product, not the entry market.
mutants.problem: Defense lawyers do not lose LOP cases for lack of a reasonable-value number. They lose because they cannot make the treating doctor's price, referral source and billing habits look bad on the stand. The billing expert is a $3-5k bespoke item, so on mid-size files it goes unordered and inflated bills get tried at face value. Claims examiners forward demand packages, often polished by plaintiff AI tools, without anyone able to read the coding. The parent idea sold a benchmark report. Florida's 768.0427 already gives a free Medicare-multiple benchmark, and hospital price files barely touch the chiropractors, pain clinics and physician-owned ASCs that do most LOP care.
mutants.solution: Order flow: firm uploads the LOP disclosure packet (letter, itemized CMS-1500/UB-04, records, factoring purchase price and referral facts where disclosed). Within 48 hours the kit returns (1) a line-item coded audit flagging unbundling, modifier-25 patterns, E/M level outliers and stacked facility fees; (2) a benchmark table with three anchors that are not hospital files: Medicare multiple, the same billing TIN's own negotiated rates from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files where it is in-network, and the factor's purchase price when disclosed; (3) a provider-bias sheet listing referral and ownership facts to ask about; (4) a two-page cross-examination outline keyed to specific bill lines for the treating-provider deposition; (5) a rebuttal outline against the plaintiff's billing expert, who will cite FAIR Health charge percentiles (the kit shows charges are what providers bill, not what anyone pays); (6) optional signed declaration; (7) optional testimony by a named coder-expert. LLM pre-codes the bill and a CPC/CCS reviews and signs in about 25 minutes, so marginal cost is roughly $40-90 per kit. Intake parsers are built for the structured demand packages plaintiff AI tools produce, so the plaintiff's arms race becomes feedstock.
mutants.why_now: Florida (2023) and Georgia (2025) reforms made LOP arrangements and amounts actually paid discoverable, and other states, including Texas, are fighting the same paid-versus-incurred battles. Plaintiff-side AI (EvenUp at a $2B+ valuation) is making bills and demands more polished, which raises defense spend on rebuttal. Payer Transparency-in-Coverage files give rates by billing TIN and NPI for free, and LLM bill extraction cuts coder time per file by more than half. None of this was workable in 2019. (Verify the current statutory status of each state before launch; I could not re-check because the search budget was exhausted.)
mutants.revenue_model: Kit $395 per file, deliberately set below the amount at which carrier litigation guidelines typically require expert pre-approval (verify the threshold in the first 10 calls). First kit free for each new firm. Signed declaration $1,900. Deposition prep $250/hr. Trial or deposition testimony $3,500/day. Panel-counsel program for firms or carrier panels at $3-6k/month for a kit quota. Target mix after 6 months: 12 firms at about 5 kits/month is about $24k/month, plus 10-15% of kits converting to declarations or testimony at 60-70% gross margin. Kits are the funnel, testimony is the margin.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a testifying coder with a public track record in that state, not coder hours or a benchmark. Judges and juries reward a credentialed ex-hospital revenue-integrity director who has survived Daubert and cross before. Every deposition transcript, Daubert or Robinson ruling, judge and outcome the company accumulates becomes a compounding cornered resource (process power plus brand) that a carrier workflow vendor cannot copy by hiring nurses. Pricing below the pre-approval threshold is also a distribution hack. Counsel can order without asking the carrier, and the carrier sees the value afterward.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-3: spend one day on the searches the parent's check could not run ('letter of protection billing expert flat fee', 'reasonable value LOP Texas Georgia') to confirm no flat-fee incumbent exists, then run 15 calls with defense lawyers to confirm the pre-approval threshold and how often the billing expert is skipped. Days 4-14: recruit two testifying coders (one Texas, one Georgia, ex-hospital or health-system revenue integrity, CPC/CCS/CPMA) plus 2 contractor coders, and one ex-panel-counsel partner as methodology advisor. Build the kit template from Medicare fee schedules and Transparency-in-Coverage files for the top payers in Houston and Atlanta, filtered to the roughly 60 CPT codes that dominate LOP bills (99203-99215, 97110-97140, 98940-98942, 72148, 73721, 62323, 64483, 64493-64495). Days 15-30: give 10 free kits on live files in exchange for a 30-minute review and a quote, then convert 3-5 firms to $395 kits and price the first declaration.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Enlyte's Demand Package Review is carrier-side workflow (nurse review, 3-10 days, no LOP framing, no signature, no testimony). This is counsel-facing work product, signed and testifiable, and Enlyte reviewers can refer files to us for the signature layer instead of us fighting them for carriers. FAIR Health is a data input and the plaintiff expert's favorite anchor, so the kit pre-rebuts it instead of selling benchmarks. EvenUp is plaintiff-only and its demand packages become our intake format. Turquoise and CLARA sell rate analytics or claims software, not signed opinions. JurisPro-style billing experts are bespoke at $3-5k and slow. We take the repeatable 80% at a tenth of the price and hand the firm an expert only when a file justifies it. Starting in Georgia and Texas avoids Florida's statutory benchmark, and using payer and Medicare anchors avoids the weak hospital-file why-now.

mutants.title: Independent Post-Reform Valuation for Medical Lien Funders
mutants.one_liner: A neutral, coder-signed valuation agent that tells LOP factoring companies and the lenders behind them what their medical receivables are worth after tort reform.
mutants.customer: Regional medical-lien funders and LOP factoring companies in Florida, Texas and Georgia that buy receivables from ortho, pain, chiropractic and ASC providers, plus the warehouse lenders and private-credit funds financing them. Buyer is the funder's CFO or head of underwriting, with the lender's credit analyst as the forcing party. First target list is 30-40 funders.
mutants.problem: Funders buy receivables at a fraction of billed charges, priced on attorney reputation and past collections. Reform changes the collateral. In Florida, 768.0427 makes the LOP, coded billing, the factoring purchase price and referral relationship disclosable and admissible, and amounts actually paid become the reference point. Cases accruing after March 2023 are only now reaching settlement, so the first post-reform collection cohort is landing on funders' books. Their lenders want borrowing-base reporting and independent collateral valuation, and no neutral standard exists. Carrier vendors, plaintiff platforms and data utilities serve everyone but the person holding the risk.
mutants.solution: Phase 1, fixed-fee 'Book Audit' in 10 business days. The funder sends a de-identified export (purchase price, coded bill lines, provider NPI, attorney, venue, dates, outcomes on closed files). Output: cohort-level expected collection and time-to-cash curves under current state rules; the top-decile at-risk receivables; a signed independent valuation letter the funder can hand to its lender or investors; and a 'bid sheet' of maximum purchase price by CPT bundle, provider type, venue and attorney tier. Phase 2: per-receivable scoring at purchase and monthly re-marking through a portal or API. Phase 3: lender-appointed valuation agent, where the warehouse lender designates and co-signs the engagement and receives monthly portfolio monitoring, like a collateral field exam. The coder bench and methodology from the parent are reused, but the output is a valuation, not a courtroom opinion.
mutants.why_now: First post-reform (Florida 2023) case cohort is resolving in 2026, so books are repricing now and lenders are asking questions. Private credit has moved into esoteric legal and medical receivables, and lenders in that class expect third-party collateral valuation. Florida's mandatory disclosure of factoring purchase price means every funder now knows its own buy price is evidence against the receivable, which forces a rethink of pricing and structure. LLM bill extraction makes coding a 2,000-line portfolio in days instead of months, with coder sampling for sign-off.
mutants.revenue_model: Book Audit $15-40k per portfolio, repeated semiannually. Subscription $3-6k/month plus $12-25 per receivable scored. Lender-facing monitoring $2-4k/month per credit facility, mandated by covenant. Illustration: 30 funders at $60k/year is about $1.8M, with upside from expanding to hospital-lien, workers' comp lien and pre-settlement receivables, and eventually independent collateral valuation for rated securitizations of medical receivables, where third-party valuation is mandatory.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Nobody has looked at LOP bills as collateral. The same benchmark that is a weapon in a deposition is a valuation input in a credit agreement, and the buyer has the best data. Funders hold the only ground-truth set of what LOP bills actually settle for, by code, provider, attorney and venue, which carriers, defense lawyers and every vendor lack. Serving funders buys that dataset and tightens every later model. The issuer-pays conflict that damaged rating agencies is solved by making the lender the appointing party and by fixed fees, like an ABL field examiner.
mutants.first_30_days: Pull UCC-1 filings (for example the Florida Secured Transaction Registry) that name medical receivables or accounts as collateral, to identify funders and the banks and credit funds financing them. Recruit two coders, one ex-ABL field examiner or credit analyst who has run a borrowing-base review, and one part-time attorney to build a rules matrix by state. Run a blind backtest pilot with 2-3 funders. They send 200-500 closed receivables with outcomes hidden, we predict the realized collection, they compare. Offer it free in exchange for permission to use the calibration. Convert the best pilot to an $18-25k Book Audit and use the result to approach that funder's lender.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Enlyte and CLARA sell to carriers, and serving receivable buyers would create channel conflict with their own customers, so they rationally will not respond. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software and does not value receivables. FAIR Health and Turquoise sell charge and rate data, which we buy as inputs. JurisPro-style expert witnesses are litigation-only and have no portfolio product or lender-facing signature. The customer set is new to all of them. The parent's Florida commoditization problem disappears because the product prices collectability and duration, not a Medicare multiple, and our moat becomes proprietary realized-collection data plus the lender relationship.

mutants.title: Subpoena-Ready Rate Cards for Lien-Based Clinics
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent by selling the coder bench to the clinics being attacked, using their own ledgers to defend their prices and build the industry's only record of what LOP care actually collects.
mutants.customer: Owner-operators of multi-location chiropractic groups, pain-management practices, ortho groups and physician-owned ASCs in Florida, Texas and Georgia that treat on letters of protection, especially those who have just received a subpoena or whose plaintiff-firm partners ask for 'defensible bills'. Wedge is 3-15 location groups in Houston, Atlanta, Orlando, Tampa and Miami. Plaintiff-firm referral managers act as influencers and channel.
mutants.problem: Reform made a clinic's pricing method, LOP arrangements, factoring and referral relationships discoverable. Owners are now deposed on how they priced a CPT code, and 'it is our standard rate' loses against a chart showing 8-15x Medicare. The honest answer is that LOP care is a credit product. The clinic waits 12-24 months, bears loss risk and often writes off 30-60% blindly at settlement. That premium is legitimate but undocumented, and nobody derives it from the clinic's own ledger. Plaintiff lawyers are not billing experts, and today's billing experts are hired after the attack.
mutants.solution: Product: LOP rate-card defense. (1) Ledger study: ingest 24-36 months of the clinic's LOP AR ledger from its practice-management export, computing realized collection per billed dollar, time-to-cash and non-recovery by code, attorney and venue. (2) Cost-of-carry model: derive a documented deferred-payment and collection-risk premium from that data. (3) Rate-card rebuild: restructure the fee schedule to a stated formula (local commercial median from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files times the documented premium) with coding hygiene fixes, written up in a dated, contemporaneous methodology memo signed by a certified coder and a health economist or CPA. (4) Deposition-defense packet for the owner and a ready declaration. (5) Annual attestation, quarterly drift check, and a per-bill 'rate-card attestation' clinics can attach. Scope excludes anything that hides referral or funding relationships. Disclosure remains counsel's job, and a healthcare regulatory lawyer reviews the offer for anti-kickback and fee-splitting risk.
mutants.why_now: Florida cases post-2023 and Georgia cases post-2025 are producing the first wave of provider subpoenas and depositions about rate-setting and referral relationships.
