Messy practice-management exports can now be normalized cheaply with LLMs, and payer Transparency-in-Coverage files make a local commercial median computable for free. Neither existed at usable cost in 2019.
mutants.revenue_model: Ledger X-ray free. Rate-card study $6.5k one-time. Monitoring and attestation $750-1,500/month per practice. Deposition prep $250/hr. Illustration: 100 clinics at $6.5k plus $900/month is about $1.7M in year one. The 10x layer is data and standard. After 150+ clinics and 30 months of ledgers, publish a quarterly 'LOP Realized Value Index' (free summary, paid detail) sold to carriers, funders, reinsurers and legislators, plus a registry that carriers pay to query. Carriers that agree to a fast lane for attested bills within the index band create a private fee schedule for the schedule-less LOP world, the way workers' comp fee schedules replaced price fights. Balance-sheet optionality later is a fund that buys attested receivables at index-based prices.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The best defense of an LOP bill is explaining why it is what it is, not proving it is cheap, and the party holding the most valuable data on real LOP value is the clinic, not the carrier or the lawyer. Selling to the attacked party is the cheapest way to acquire that data, since a subpoena is a fear purchase with budget behind it. Providers will hand ledgers to a neutral appraiser but never to a carrier vendor, which is counter-positioning that Enlyte and CLARA cannot copy without alienating carriers. The credibility risk is issuer-pays conflict, mitigated by algorithmic pass/fail thresholds, a published methodology, a visible fail rate, a carrier-side advisory seat and a firewall from any case-specific testimony.
mutants.first_30_days: Pick Houston and Orlando/Tampa. Build a list of 60 lien-based groups from provider directories and plaintiff-firm referral networks, and approach through state chiropractic and pain-medicine associations and referral managers at plaintiff firms. Offer the free 'ledger X-ray': send an AR export and in 5 days get a one-page showing billed versus collected, time-to-cash and the five lines an expert would attack first. Sign 5 paid studies at $6.5k within 60 days. In parallel, hold 3 carrier claims-executive calls to test whether an attested schedule would be accepted in pre-suit, and one call with a healthcare regulatory attorney on structure and disclaimers.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Enlyte and CLARA serve carriers and cannot sell to providers without channel conflict, and providers will not share ledgers with them. FAIR Health measures charges and allowed amounts, while we measure realized LOP collections and carry cost, so the index complements it and rebuts the plaintiff's usual-and-customary anchor. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software with no rate-card defense and is a possible channel partner for its firms' referral networks. Turquoise does payer-contracting analytics, not lien care, and is a data supplier with some entrant risk to watch. The closest direct substitute is per-case billing experts (including plaintiff-side JurisPro-type experts). They are hired after the attack and sell single-case declarations, while this is contemporaneous, subscription-based, data-backed documentation that carries more weight than a declaration created after the fact.

mutants.title: Consent Ledger for Land-Scheme Family Cohorts
mutants.one_liner: A cohort-priced heir-consent ledger sold to the family 'treasurer' of heirs from ONE 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme, with a partner law firm as the legal entity of record and a recurring Title Watch on top.
mutants.customer: The 'family treasurer': the salaried eldest or most solvent sibling (30-55, in Nairobi, Nakuru, Dallas or Dubai) of a family whose parent or grandparent was an allottee or member of one named land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county (pick one scheme in Murang'a, Kiambu, Nakuru or Trans Nzoia through the founder's own church/alumni/clan network). Distribution partners are the scheme's officials and welfare committee. One partner law firm is the entity of record for all legal work.
mutants.problem: Judges flagged three flaws in the parent: thin unit economics (field trips per single estate eat the KES 15-25k fee), the Advocates Act risk of a non-lawyer company selling a 'court-ready bundle' (from memory, unverified), and unproven diaspora willingness to pay. The underlying pain is real but narrower than 'succession': the blocker is proving that all 8-20 heirs were found, asked and agreed, and getting them to sign at all. There is also a sharper trigger than paperwork guilt: land in a dead man's name is an easy target for forged transfers and brokers, and absent children fear waking up to find it sold. A generic 'succession kit' has neither the density to be profitable nor a legal shape that survives scrutiny.
mutants.solution: Three steps, each cheap to buy. (0) 'Title Check', KES 1,500 over WhatsApp: photo of the title or parcel number, official search (about KES 500 fee, verify), LLM read of the result, one-page plain-language answer: registered owner, is that person dead, who must be involved. (1) 'Consent Ledger', KES 18k (KES 14k cohort price when 8+ estates from the same chief's location are booked): Kenyan name-variant-reconciled heir map, list of required consents, and a live status board the treasurer shares in the family WhatsApp group ('9 of 14 heirs signed, 3 outstanding, reasons'). A home-area agent runs one scheduled 'signing day' per chief's location per month for chief's-letter requests, ID copies, thumbprints and video consent; heirs elsewhere sign by ID-video on WhatsApp witnessed by the nearest agent. Output is a non-legal 'Consent and Kinship Evidence Pack' with a dispute flag (silent heir, second household, contested claim). The partner law firm receives the pack through a case-management seat, drafts, files and shepherds the case, and bills its own scale fee directly; the company never drafts affidavits or quotes legal fees. (2) 'Title Watch', KES 4k per parcel per year: alerts on registry changes plus a caution/restriction workflow run through the advocate. Asset discovery (SACCO, coop, UFAA letters) is a flat add-on sold only after grant, since UFAA beneficiary claims need the confirmed grant first.
mutants.why_now: LLMs now read scanned titles, IDs and share certificates and reconcile Kenyan name variants for cents a page, and drafting copilots (Wakili-Intel appeared July 2026 as a hobby project) are commoditising the paperwork, so the scarce, defensible piece moves to field evidence and multi-heir consent, which is still custom work. The settlement-scheme allottee generation is dying now. WhatsApp Business plus M-Pesa/card make small cross-border payments routine, and digitised searches (Ardhisasa; coverage to be verified) cut registry running. None of this worked in 2019: reading messy scans and chatting in Swahili and English at this cost did not exist.
mutants.revenue_model: Ladder per estate: KES 1.5k Title Check, then KES 18k ledger (14k at cohort density), then KES 3k flat advocate seat fee per file (software and case management charge, explicitly not a fee split; verify with counsel), then KES 4k/yr Title Watch, then KES 5k asset-discovery add-on after grant. Assumption to test: at cohort density, field plus search plus ops cost is about KES 7-8k per ledger versus KES 12-15k for one-off estates, giving roughly 45-55% gross margin and about KES 26-30k first-year revenue per estate. A county team (coordinator, 2 agents, share of ops, about KES 3M a year) breaks even near 200 estates a year, which one large scheme can supply. Title Watch gives recurring revenue that the parent lacked.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The unit of production is not the estate but the chief's location. Neighbouring estates in one scheme share the same registry, chief, original allottee list, surnames and often the same feuds, so every ledger makes the next one cheaper and better (name-variant dictionary, known-disputer flags, chief relationships). That density economy is invisible to per-estate advocates and to national software. Second, the treasurer is buying a status board, not paperwork: it turns family guilt and pressure into visible progress that nudges holdout siblings. Third, fear of land-grabbing is the purchase trigger, so sell 'protect it' first and 'sort the succession' second.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: pick one scheme and one county through your own family, church or alumni network; sign one partner law firm as entity of record on a one-page engagement letter (advocate bills the client directly; company charges a flat seat fee). Days 7-20: launch the WhatsApp 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' Title Check at KES 1,500 in the scheme's clan and welfare WhatsApp groups and in diaspora groups for that county; run 40 checks. Days 20-30: convert to 10 pre-sold Consent Ledgers at pilot price, of which at least 8 in one chief's location; schedule the first group signing day. Core metrics: days from intake to all heirs signed, percent of heirs signed on the first visit, and check-to-ledger conversion. Kill test: fewer than 3 of 40 checkers buy a ledger.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Fixed-fee advocates (the only direct competitor) become the channel: they receive consent-complete, dispute-triaged files at zero acquisition cost and keep all legal fees, while the company sells only the field and evidence layer they cannot profitably do at scale fees (chasing 14 heirs across three counties). Luru and Wakili-Intel are zero-star software with no field agents, consent capture or advocates, and drafting is exactly what we do not sell. UFAA is used only after grant as a flat add-on, not a lead product. Ardhisasa and court e-filing are systems we file into, not substitutes; even if Ardhisasa adds guided transmission it will not collect thumbprints from scattered heirs. Defensibility comes from cohort density and the per-scheme kinship dictionary (cornered resource) plus counter-positioning against advocates who cannot make per-heir chasing pay.

mutants.title: SACCO-Financed Succession Desk, Paid on Milestones
mutants.one_liner: A white-label succession desk that payroll SACCOs offer their members: a check-off-repaid 'estate clearing loan' goes into a milestone escrow, and the company earns only as each case step is proven.
mutants.customer: The payer and channel is the mid-size payroll or sector SACCO (5k-100k members: teachers, health workers, county staff, police and prison staff) in central and western Kenya, sold to the CEO and credit committee. End users are two groups: salaried members (30-55) whose deceased parent's land is still in a dead name, and heirs of deceased members whose deposits and shares are stuck without a grant. The diaspora child is no longer the only payer.
mutants.problem: SACCOs hold two stuck pools. First, deposits and shares of deceased members that cannot be paid out cleanly until heirs produce a grant or agree among themselves (many SACCOs allow small nominee payouts; larger balances and family disputes stall; exact limits to verify): a governance headache, audit query and source of angry families. Second, living members who would borrow large development or mortgage loans against family land, but the land is in a dead person's name so the SACCO cannot take security. Members themselves cannot find a KES 100-250k lump sum for advocate, fees and travel, and distrust strangers who take money for land paperwork, yet they have salaries that can be deducted at source.
mutants.solution: The SACCO brands a 'Succession Desk'; the company runs it. Wedge (sellable in 30 days, no SACCO cash outlay): 'Deceased-Member Deposit Clearing'. The SACCO gives a letter of introduction and the list of stuck estates; the company does WhatsApp intake, heir map, consents and field work with a fixed-fee advocate panel; heirs consent in writing to a flat fee deducted from the released deposits. Stage 2, after three or more cases close: 'Estate Clearing Loan' for living members, sized KES 60-250k and repaid by payroll check-off. Proceeds sit in a SACCO-held milestone escrow released at proven steps: heir map and consent pack complete, petition filed and gazetted, confirmation of grant, transmission registered. Advocate fees (from a pre-agreed schedule) and the company's fee are paid from escrow to each party directly against milestones, so the member never hands cash to a stranger and the company never holds client money. At the end the SACCO has a pledgeable title (with heirs' consents to charge) and can pre-approve a development or mortgage loan.
mutants.why_now: Payroll SACCOs now run digital member ledgers, USSD and M-Pesa collections, and face competition from banks and digital lenders for their best salaried members, so they want secured, sticky products. Regulator attention on SACCO governance and deceased or dormant member balances (SASRA; verify current rules) makes stuck estates a board-level problem. LLM intake and heir mapping cut the cost of a case enough that a flat KES 12-18k fee works inside a loan. The succession backlog from 1960s-80s allottees is at its peak. Without cheap AI intake the desk would have needed paralegal armies, so this business model did not pencil out in 2019.
mutants.revenue_model: Contingent milestone fees of KES 12-18k per estate case, split over the four milestones (for example 40% at consents plus filing, 60% at grant and transmission), funded either from released deposits (deceased-member cases) or from estate clearing loan proceeds via escrow. The company takes no interest and no percentage of estate value. Flat per-loan bounty of KES 3-5k when a cleared title later secures a SACCO loan. After a successful pilot, a white-label desk fee of about KES 150-250k a year per SACCO. Illustration: 10 SACCOs at 100 cases a year each is roughly KES 15M in case fees plus about KES 2M in platform fees (about US$130k), with the SACCOs, not the company, carrying credit risk. The SACCO earns loan interest and clears a liability.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Affordability and trust, not awareness, are the barriers, and the SACCO uniquely owns what neither an advocate nor a startup can: payroll check-off (repayment that costs almost nothing to collect), a welfare touchpoint at the exact moment of a death, and a balance-sheet motive (release stuck deposits, make land pledgeable). The estate clearing loan turns a scary lump sum into a monthly deduction, and the milestone escrow turns a scary stranger into a vendor who is only paid for proven progress. The SACCO's deceased-member float is an embarrassing liability nobody currently sells a fix for.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: list 40 SACCOs whose managers you can reach through personal, church, alumni and county networks (teachers', hospital, county-staff SACCOs first). Ask one question: how many deceased-member accounts are pending succession and how many shillings are stuck? Days 10-20: sign two advocates to a fixed-fee panel schedule and draft a one-page pilot contract: SACCO letter of introduction, member-consented flat fee deducted from released deposits, no SACCO cash outlay, so it fits within a CEO's delegated authority and does not need a board vote. Days 20-30: sign one SACCO for 15-20 stuck estates, start intake on the first 5 by WhatsApp, and publish an anonymised 'stuck member deposits' figure to open the next SACCOs. In parallel, draft the estate clearing loan term sheet with that SACCO's credit committee. Metric: days from intake to consents complete, and shillings released per case.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Fixed-fee advocates (the direct competitor) sit on the panel and are paid directly from escrow, so the desk is their referral source rather than their rival, and no fee is split with a non-lawyer. Luru and Wakili-Intel have no distribution, field agents or financing and are zero-star hobby projects. UFAA is unaffected because the desk clears the SACCO's own liabilities, not UFAA assets. Ardhisasa and e-filing are systems the panel files into. Competing on a different axis (who pays and how): individual advocates cannot offer financing or escrow; banks will not run rural field operations; SACCOs will not build LLM intake and consent ops in-house. Switching costs come from integration with the SACCO's loan system, panel and escrow, and it does not depend on the parent's unproven diaspora willingness to pay.

mutants.title: Mzee's Testament: Family Land Councils Before Death
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of untangling the dead man's land after the funeral, hold a video-witnessed Family Land Council this December while the parent is alive and every heir is home, lock it into a will, family agreement, capacity certificate and time-locked vault, and grow the format into a registry of family land intent.
mutants.customer: Diaspora and urban children (30-55) with living rural parents aged 65-90 who hold unsubdivided family land. The child pays in September-November for a December council, but the parent is the legal client of the partner advocate. Later payers are SACCOs, lenders and insurers who buy verified family land plans (with family consent), and churches and clan associations as channels.
mutants.problem: After death, succession takes 1-3 years, is contested and costs heirs dearly (parent's figures). Every year of delay means heirs die, feuds harden, and evidence disappears. Children abroad only get all siblings into one compound at Christmas. Parents avoid 'death talk' and fear that gifting land makes them dependants. Where informal wills exist they are often unwitnessed or challenged for lack of capacity or undue influence, and daughters and second households are frequently excluded by custom, which produces litigation later. No one sells a cheap, provable record of what the parent actually wanted, agreed by all children while the parent can still speak.
mutants.solution: 'Family Land Council': a one-day facilitated event at the family home in the 20 Dec to 5 Jan window, prepared in October-November by WhatsApp intake, an official title search, a heir list including second households and a parcel sketch. On the day a team of three attends: a facilitator, a partner advocate who acts for the parent and first meets the parent alone, and a videographer, plus a clinician's capacity assessment on site or the same week. Outputs: (1) the parent's recorded, parent-alone statement of wishes; (2) a Family Land Agreement signed by all adult children in person or by video (allocation, parent's lifetime use and residence, burial ground, provision for daughters and widows); (3) a properly witnessed will drafted by the advocate; (4) an encrypted Family Land Vault holding video, documents and a machine-readable Family Land Plan, released to named heirs only when a death certificate is uploaded and two heirs confirm. Optional track: transfer by gift or subdivision with the parent's use protected, through surveyor, Land Control Board consent and registry, which skips the court queue entirely. The exact legal structure (gift versus will, consent requirements, stamp duty treatment) must be confirmed with Kenyan counsel.
mutants.why_now: December 2026 is about ten weeks away and diaspora flights are booked in October-November, so the product's launch window is literal. The allottee generation is 65-90 now: each year removes some of the people whose testimony is the whole point. LLMs, phone video and e-signature make an evidence pack cheap, and drafting is commoditising (Wakili-Intel, July 2026) while witnessing, capacity evidence and convening a family are not. Remittances of roughly US$5bn a year (parent's figure, verify) show families already pay to 'sort out the land' from abroad. This would have worked in 2019 only as a boutique law-firm service; the cost of running councils at scale with intake, video and vault software is new.
mutants.revenue_model: Council package: KES 40k service fee (about US$310) for pre-work, facilitation, video and capacity evidence and vault setup, pilot price KES 25k. The advocate's will and agreement drafting (KES 15-25k, assumption) is billed directly by the advocate to the parent as client, and the clinician's fee is passed through at cost. Vault subscription KES 3k a year per family (annual refresh video on the parent's birthday, updates for births, marriages and deaths), target 60% attach. Gift or subdivision track: KES 20k service fee on top of surveyor, Land Control Board and registry costs at cost. Later B2B: per-verified-plan fees from SACCOs, lenders and insurers, with consent. Year one aim: 50-60 councils, about KES 2M revenue at roughly 55% gross margin (cost about KES 14-18k per council), validating the model rather than making money. Scale-up: church and clan chapters delivering 500+ councils per December.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The paying child is the likeliest future litigant, so the product only works if the parent is the client: parent alone on tape, an independent advocate, a capacity certificate and a cooling-off period. That evidence can only be produced while the parent is alive, which is why no post-death service, however good, can replace it. December is the one moment all 8-20 heirs are physically together and emotionally invested, so the coordination problem that costs a year after death costs a day before it. The inversion also turns a one-off dead-paperwork job into a living, recurring relationship (vault refresh, births and deaths) whose data compounds into a standard-setting registry of family land intent.
mutants.first_30_days: October: recruit two advocates who do wills and agree a parent-as-client engagement letter, and one clinician for capacity assessments. Run a dry-run council for a friendly family (Murang'a or Kakamega) to time the day and script the parent-alone interview. Launch a landing page and WhatsApp booking with 30 December slots at the KES 25k pilot price and a 30% M-Pesa deposit, sold through diaspora Facebook and WhatsApp groups, church and alumni networks, with a free 'Family Land Map' quiz as lead magnet. Recruit and train four facilitators (paralegals, community mobilisers, retired chief's assistants). Targets: 15 paid slots by 30 October and 30 by end of November. The riskiest assumption is that parents agree, so measure the parent-consent rate among families whose child pays (target above 60%).
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Advocates who draft wills (the direct competitor) sell one document to one client in an office; the council sells a convened, witnessed, family-wide process and evidence pack, with the advocate as paid partner and no fee split. Luru scores post-death readiness and Wakili-Intel drafts pleadings for advocates, both software, both after death, neither with field or convening capability. UFAA is a post-death channel; Ardhisasa and court e-filing are bypassed on the gift track and used on the succession track. Incumbents do not respond because advocates earn more from contested post-death matters and courts, the Public Trustee and funeral insurers do not run family meetings. The main threat is a government wills registry, which the format, vault and process still complement. Defensibility: data on family plans accepted by chiefs, SACCOs and lenders (network economies, cornered resource) and process power in running parent-safe councils.
